#4227. Trees Hate You Review: You’ll Enjoy Hating Them Back

Trees Hate You uses unpredictable traps and cartoon-style humor in a short, silly rage game, though its bugs and limited challenge may frustrate some.

It’s a very odd time in gaming where we’re seeing a lot more games coming out than ever before. Some are better than others, but many seem to simply have some fun and interesting premises that draw you in.

One such game would be Trees Hate You, which is a ridiculous rage game about being targeted by trees. Sounds like it shouldn’t be very good, but surprisingly the game’s Looney Tunes-esque approach to mechanics makes it an enjoyable game.

I played the game for around four hours, though a speed run could be significantly quicker, and came away enjoying most of my time with the game. It isn’t a perfect game, but it is a fun game, especially if you’re just looking for a silly little rage game.

It’s not a complex or complicated game in all reality, but that’s part of its charm. You play as a person who’s being hunted by trees for some reason or another and must navigate through several locations to finally reach your destination.

There’s very little in the way of story since virtually all of the information presented is through the visuals of the game. You’ll need to make your way through many dangerous traps that will change, sometimes seemingly at random.

It isn’t a perfect game, but it is a fun game, especially if you’re just looking for a silly little rage game.

There are four “levels,” three of which are separated into smaller sections to make it more digestible. Each section has a central theme and introduces some new trees while finding creative ways to make you scream obscenities.

It’s a pretty short and sweet game that culminates in a very, very odd ending. There aren’t really any abilities to get or anything to make the game easier. From the outset of the game, you’ve got your movement buttons and whatever brain power you can muster.

Super Meat Boy 3D is still the same series you love, now with even more ways and directions to die over and over. Here's our full review!

For a lot of rage games, each section of the game is stagnant so that you can learn from your mistakes and grow smarter. In this game, that entire ideology is completely thrown out the window, and it makes it much more interesting to play.

For almost every section of the game, when you die you end up back at the last checkpoint, but you’ll notice that something might be a little different. Sometimes it’s a new tree popping up along the path or a new path entirely.

This seemed to change at random upon death, and figuring out how to handle the changes added a new layer to the game. For some, it’s going to be frustrating in a different way, since it does change, meaning memorizing the path isn’t particularly helpful.

I thoroughly enjoyed that change of pace. As a big fan of great roguelikes, seeing that sort of game design appear here gave me pause at first until I got used to it. It managed to keep the game fresh despite the short run time.

There was a lot about this game that I thoroughly enjoyed, but there is no denying that the game felt way too short. Perhaps that was because I simply had played through some other rage games recently that prepared me for this, but still I felt it could’ve been a much longer experience.

Being a short experience isn’t too bad, as there are a few things that you can grind for if you really want, such as coins and hats, but at the end of the day this is a game you could beat in a single session. I suppose I was hoping to have a bit more oomph out of the game, though what we did get was more than fine.

There is a challenge mode that changes up some of the levels and makes things a bit more complicated with more traps and threats, but the levels will always remain the same between deaths. It was nice to provide the option to give players more bang for their buck.

The game doesn’t really waste any time on things that aren’t humorous or torturing you, which is a big bonus. As I approached the end, though, I had hoped the game would surprise me and get a bit longer or more ridiculous, but there was no such luck.

If you're looking for experiences that aren't artificially prolonged, check out these ten fastest Metroidvanias to 100%.

Video games are not often known for their sense of humor, and even less so for their ability to utilize visual gags. Trees Hate You has decided to right this wrong by making what effectively feels like a Looney Tunes episode into an entire game.

At first it was just some slight things, moments that felt naturally funny because of the tension and ridiculousness of the game. That changed after a few levels when trees began to do whatever they pleased, seemingly just to mess with me.

There is one tree in particular that embodies this ideology entirely. One tree blocks your path early on in the game by bending at insane angles to force you in another direction. This same tree will do this for the entirety of the game.

You’ll come across a path sometime later, and suddenly out of the sky the tree will reach down and block your path. This was incredibly idiotic and amazing. I had to stop and try it again just to make sure I could see what exactly was going on.

It’s a pretty hilarious game, especially when you run into those annoyingly funny moments that make you feel like you’ve been outsmarted by the trees. Even if you’re not a big fan of this kind of humor, it’s still enjoyable to see all the unique ways the trees manage to get you.

This is going to be something that I think gets to be a little divisive amongst people who play the game. On the one hand, the game isn’t quite as difficult as it could be, but on the other hand, the changing mechanics could make it more difficult for some.

I would’ve liked to see the game be a bit more difficult the first go around, but there is a challenge mode. It sort of balances out, giving everyone a chance to enjoy something about the game, but there were only a few sections that really got to me.

It’s a pretty hilarious game, especially when you run into those annoyingly funny moments that make you feel like you’ve been outsmarted by the trees.

It feels like the game is more about trial and error rather than conquering any difficult mechanics, and that’s more than okay, but it does take away some of the feeling of accomplishment. In reality, it feels like the game is more designed to watch others fail than to be played itself.

Ironically, there’s a lot of time to sit with what happens when you die in some crazy fashion. You’ll respawn at a checkpoint with virtually no risk, meaning you’ll never need to complete a past section a second time.

Trees Hate You is an interesting rage game that leans more heavily into the absurdity of the genre than the actual rage. Still, it’s a hilarious and ridiculously fun game. You’re going to walk away from the game having enjoyed yourself immensely despite some of the more pressing issues. There are annoying bugs that will force you to start from a prior checkpoint, but all in all, the game is a very good time.

If you’re looking for a true video game challenge, I suggest you try these ten hardest Metroidvanias to 100%.

We’ve scoured dozens of tech products, tabletop games, collectibles, and more to select and highlight some of the coolest items we found this year.

We recommended the Board shortly after its launch, but with its expanded game library and lower price than first-adopter rates, this holiday season is an ideal time to make the leap. This family-friendly platform features original games that sit comfortably between the digital and physical divide. The horizontally placed screen shows the backdrop of one of the several included games, or the sold-separately add-on games that have popped in since launch. Each game has its own real physical play pieces that interact with the action onscreen, often in innovative and charming ways. Think of it as the best of both worlds between board games and video games, and you’ll get what they’re shooting for here. $399

Few additions to the latest Dungeons & Dragons rules pack as much punch and value as this new expansion, focusing on ways to develop further and evolve the use of magic across your tabletop gaming sessions. Sega has packed in OutRun, Turbo OutRun, OutRunners, and Power Drift. If old-school racing isn’t your thing, look for cabinets that run the gamut from Pac-Man to Joust to Claw Machines. $629.99

The long-running Nendoroid figures continue to be an attractive but still affordable choice for building collections across numerous fan-favorite series. There are somewhere around 2000 characters at this point! New entries like the Genshin Impact collection make a strong case for the line. The look is chibi, the quality is excellent, poseability is high, and customizable face and accessory parts let you change up your display over time. $46

We’ve previously sung the praises of Libernovo’s versatile approach to an ergonomic gaming chair, which includes a lumbar stretch functionality, a steady recline option for comfortable pushback without sudden shifts, and dynamically adjusting parts as you move through your day. The Maxis line does all that, but addresses one of the fundamental problems for at least some users with the original – it wasn’t big enough. With features like a wider base and longer headrest reach, the Maxis aims to provide the same comfort to the players who are tall or wide enough to need the extra breathing room. $1119

If you’re the player on your team who likes to have easy access to soundboards and real-time voice changing, the Key Pocket could be just the ticket. This small device straps onto your phone for mobile play, but it’s also compatible with consoles, Discord, Twitch, or just about any place you want to tweak audio on the fly. A free tier gives you access to some voice-changing and sounds, while a separate subscription opens up hundreds of thousands of additional options. But be warned: we can’t help you after your friends abandon you for that baby voice you won’t stop using. $99

The question of the best bang for your buck in modern consoles has become extraordinarily complicated, especially as tech prices have soared in recent years. There’s no right answer, but Sony’s high-end machine walks the line of offering extremely high-tier performance without escalating to even higher-priced gaming PCs. Higher and more consistent frame rates than on standard PS5, advanced ray tracing, and an increasing number of games that feature enhanced PSSR image options all add up to a better gaming experience, if you’re ready to make the significant price jump. $900

If the gamer in your life is looking for a stylish, understated way to express their love of the hobby, Anicorn’s designer watch collaboration with PlayStation could be a standout option. Available in black and a slick silver/white combo, the minimalist timepiece includes the familiar face buttons of Sony’s controller encased in an oil-injection display so they slowly and freely float across the watch as you move. $250

It’s a safe bet you’ve at least seen the popular Shashibo puzzle cubes by this point. We’ve been fans of their brain-teasing, fidgety fun for some time. Battle Shapes takes the core concept – reshaping the box into various distinct magnetically-locked shapes – and extends it into a timed game experience, playable solo or head-to-head. By targeting specific shapes, you significantly improve your speed with the toy, and scannable QR codes on the cards offer clear tutorials for each shape so you can prep for competition. $50

While the vast majority of gamers looking for good personal audio are going to be okay with a larger set of cans over their ears, We know more than a few players for whom that’s a definite no – for comfort, awareness of surrounding sounds, or other reasons. The Arc 5 earbuds aim to solve for that, with an over-ear design that feels extremely comfortable. And because they sit on the ear, you can still hear what’s going on around you. While that limits some aspects of the final sound quality, the inclusion of THX certification, Dolby Atmos optimization, and Dynamic Bass Enhancement helps to ensure audio is still very strong. $230

Across Lego’s many recent themes, Tolkien’s legendarium has offered some stellar sets. The largest yet is the capital of Gondor, with an astonishing 8,278 pieces and a height of roughly two feet. The castle/city build is impressive, featuring tons of interesting angles and turns. The finished product aims to offer the best of both worlds in presentation – a microscale representation of the front façade and a reverse minifigure-scale Hall of Kings. We especially like the inclusion of Denethor’s cherry tomatoes. $650

The original Azul is often cited as a foundational entry in modern board gaming. The “Kids” versions of celebrated titles aren’t always a sure bet, but this one holds up to scrutiny. Azul Kids lowers the complexity threshold but keeps the foundational strategic thinking. Players lay out uniquely shaped tiles into mosaic frameworks in colorful, appealing patterns; the basic concept of the original inspiration is clear, and kids as young as five can grasp and enjoy the fun. $25

Many corners of the collecting world have embraced the fun (and frequent despair) of blind boxes, where you never know exactly who you’ll get in a given series. Funism has a strong track record for quality, offering adorable smaller figures like their latest line of Evangelion collectibles. Each figure stands nearly four inches and features both human characters and mecha. You can buy singles and roll the dice, or purchase larger sets with a no-duplicates guarantee, which can save a lot of heartache if you’re trying to line your whole shelf. $21

If you’re going to spring for a high-end keyboard for PC gaming, it’s important that you like the feel of the keys. The slightly smaller overall 75% size profile of this Blackwidow has no impact on the great feel of typing – a clear highlight for the unit. The customizable, colored backlights are also a big selling point, as is the side command dial and built-in OLED display, which can be tweaked to show PC performance, GIFs, lighting brightness, and more. It’s a strong contender in a crowded field, and justifies its price with both comfort and customizability. $300

Beautiful, vibrant art and a refreshing take on the classic area-control board game genre are the two strongest reasons to take a close look at Wroth. Players control one of five races vying for supremacy across a conflict-ridden peninsula. Factions are asymmetric, so everyone has unique capabilities, and that adds significant replayability. Players roll and draft dice, allowing distinct actions that move the game forward. And move it does; unlike many games of this ilk, Wroth can be learned quickly and played to completion in a little over an hour. $65

Console and computer hardware prices are skyrocketing with no sign of slowing, and perhaps as a result, retro gaming handhelds are gaining popularity. Many quality devices are available, but what sets the Evercade Nexus apart is its officially licensed game cartridges. Imagine the nostalgic joy of a Game Boy, but with a cartridge that includes both Banjo-Kazooie and Tooie. The cartridge boxes even include manuals. For fans of physical media, Evercade Nexus is a great option. $199

This tiny USB-C plug-in (with included USB-A adapter) solves a bunch of audio challenges in one uniform device. It offers high-resolution Bluetooth transmission on iPhone, high-bitrate audio transmission to compatible LDAC headphones, enables high-quality Bluetooth output from your PC, and even low-latency Bluetooth audio on PS5 and Switch. In short, it takes a huge number of products with a USB port and ensures a dynamic Bluetooth audio connection with relative ease. $99

The original MV6 is a familiar sight on streams thanks to its clear voice reproduction and overall ease of use. Shure has built on that success with the Gen 2, offering an excellent standalone mic that doesn’t break the bank. Available in black or white, the Gen 2 features a handy auto-level mode that keeps volume even as you adjust your own amplitude, an adjustable denoiser for your space, a longer cable for out-of-the-box convenience, and three presets for plug-and-play use. In short, it’s an excellent choice if you want great performance without needing an audio engineering degree. $169

XR Glasses are still fighting for awareness, but once you try them, it’s easy to see why the concept is on the rise. Viture’s Pro 2 makes an impressive case for adoption, with a competitive price point, comfortable wear, and a giant 146-inch screen that floats in front of your face for gaming or work on your PC or phone. The display is crisp, bright, and impressive, even as the glasses are light and easy to use. With a mobile dock mini (sold separately), you can even snap onto a Switch 2 with ease and start playing instantly. $299

Role-playing gamers have several excellent universal systems to pick between when considering a story or campaign idea that might fall outside traditional genre staples. Among many good options, Cypher stands out as one of the very best. The system uses a rules-light, narrative-focused approach that prioritizes player-driven storytelling across everything from hard sci-fi to superheroes to intrigue- driven espionage. This is the corebook that’s needed to run and play the full system; additional books only add options. $50

As gamers have continually migrated toward personal audio that can rock amazing sound without disturbing the whole house, high-end premium headphones have become a dangerously competitive space. Turtle Beach meets that challenge head-on, with a robust option that sounds beautiful in use. The Stealth Pro II boasts the slick ability to wirelessly switch between different devices, which is awesome if you’re one of those players who regularly jumps between platforms to play your favorite titles. Like the whole category, it’s a lot to spend on a headset, but Dolby Atmos, active noise cancellation, and 60mm dual drivers all add up to a powerful argument. $300

With an increasing number of top-tier console and PC games like Resident Evil Village, No Man’s Sky, and Dead Cells now available on iOS, not to mention the consistent quality of Apple Arcade, Apple phones remain the best mobile platform for gaming. The 18 Pro Max phone has implemented a number of tweaks that strengthen the platform, including higher memory, much faster graphics processing, impressive HDR performance, and notably improved battery life, all adding up to a gaming experience that is working hard to justify your playtime when away from home. Starting at $1299

SteelSeries is best known for its strong audio line-up, but its push into premium-tier controllers exhibits a similar flair for quality and usability. The new Aeon Pro has a lot to recommend it as your go-to Xbox, PC, or mobile choice. The two included batteries (one of which can always be charging in the dock) ensure essentially unlimited playtime. The full-pull or hair triggers and buttons are clicky and satisfying, and the Hall Effect thumbsticks are built to minimize any drift. Textured handgrips and overall heft are ideal. And an onboard OLED lets you adjust profiles and button assignments, switch between platforms, and check battery at a glance. $260

Valve’s pricey VR headset isn’t a revolution in the medium, but the company has been invested in the technology since its inception. As a result, the Steam Frame is a very good, very comfortable headset. Like its competition, the Quest, its best use is playing games locally on the headset, and Steam’s library is vast and interesting. Wireless connected play to a powerful PC is also well done, but currently the included Wireless Adapter is not fully compatible with the Steam Machine – a baffling limitation we were shocked to confirm. VR is an expensive sub-hobby within video games, but Steam Frame is among the best ways to explore and enjoy it. $1059

Many of the coolest “gaming lights” focus on the flexibility and fun of bright RGB customization. While we’re fans of that aesthetic, it leaves others out in the cold who might want something a bit more natural. The Elements hex panels feature a natural wood-inspired panel, customizable “scenes” like a campfire glow, and can react to both music and touch, with adjustable ambient white light to keep the vibe relaxed. $200

Kyle Hilliard contributed to this article.

#4225. A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math

For some children, learning math is much more difficult than it is for their classmates. Even when they practice and receive instruction, they may continue to struggle with problems that other children their age can solve more easily. Researchers are now uncovering clues about why these difficulties persist, and the answers may involve more than an understanding of numbers.

One possible explanation lies in differences in how the brain selects and manages strategies for solving problems. A new study from Stanford University suggests that children with persistent math difficulties may have trouble adjusting their approach when faced with different mathematical challenges. The researchers also identified distinctive patterns of brain activity associated with these struggles.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, come from research led by Oliver Lasnick and colleagues at Stanford University. Their work focused on children with a condition that causes ongoing difficulty with mathematical problem solving (developmental dyscalculia). Although the condition has been recognized for years, scientists are still working to understand the specific thinking processes and brain mechanisms that contribute to it.

Why Some Children Struggle With Math Strategies

To investigate these challenges, the Stanford team studied 68 children between the ages of 8 and 10. They examined how the children approached math problems, how effectively they used different strategies, and how their brain activity related to their performance.

Solving a math problem often requires more than knowing numbers or remembering arithmetic facts. Children must also decide which approach will work best. For example, a child might count individual numbers to find an answer or use a more efficient method based on a familiar mathematical relationship. As problems become more difficult, the ability to recognize when a different strategy is needed can become increasingly important.

The researchers found that children with developmental dyscalculia were generally less effective at using different mathematical strategies than children without the condition. They took longer to shift from one method to another and were less responsive when the difficulty of a problem changed.

Another important difference involved learning to choose better strategies over time. While other children became more effective at selecting appropriate approaches, those with developmental dyscalculia did not show the same improvement. This suggests that their difficulties may involve not only performing calculations but also deciding how to approach a problem in the first place.

Brain Activity Reveals New Clues to Math Difficulties

The researchers also examined patterns of brain activity to better understand what might be happening behind these behavioral differences.

They discovered that activity within a particular brain system differed between children with developmental dyscalculia and those who were more skilled at selecting and using math strategies. These neural patterns were not simply unrelated differences. They could also predict how effectively children counted and how well they switched between approaches when solving problems.

The findings highlight the possible importance of several mental abilities that extend beyond mathematics itself. These include attention, memory, and cognitive flexibility, which is the ability to adjust thinking or behavior when circumstances change.

Such abilities are part of what researchers often call executive functions. These mental processes help people organize information, stay focused on a task, hold relevant details in mind, and change plans when an approach is not working. In mathematics, they can help a child keep track of numbers, compare possible solutions, and recognize when to try a different method.

The Stanford findings suggest that difficulties involving these processes may contribute to the development of dyscalculia. Differences in brain activity may also help explain why some children have persistent trouble choosing and changing problem-solving strategies.

However, the observed connections do not establish that the brain activity differences directly cause the condition. They provide new evidence about the cognitive and neural processes associated with these mathematical difficulties.

Understanding Why Math Struggles Differ Between Children

An important conclusion is that developmental dyscalculia does not appear to involve one simple problem shared by every affected child. Instead, different children may experience difficulties involving several interacting mental processes.

As Lasnick explains, "Importantly, this study also emphasizes the individual variability observed in dyscalculia, further demonstrating that the disorder reflects cognitive and neural dysfunction across multiple processes."

By connecting children's mathematical behavior with measurable differences in brain activity, the research offers a more detailed picture of why math can be persistently challenging for some students.

The findings also point toward the importance of looking beyond whether a child gets the correct answer. Understanding how children choose strategies, adapt to more difficult problems, and manage the mental demands of mathematics could ultimately help researchers develop better ways to identify and support those with developmental dyscalculia.

Materials provided by Society for Neuroscience. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4224. Love and Deepspace 5.0 update brings together all five love interests for the first time

Love and Deepspace is getting a big update to celebrate its second anniversary, and there's a lot to dig through.

If you can believe it, Love and Deepspace is almost two-years-old, and Infold Games is celebrating the moment in a few major ways. The Throne of Eros update brings the game up to version 5.0, and it’s one for fans of all love interests.

For one, this is the first time all five of them are brought together. The update is also adding some important new features, alongside anniversary events, and more.

Throne of Eros also doubles as the new Wish Pool, which is the one that has all of the game’s love interests in a single banner. This is a limited-time affair, of course, but it’s not the only thing you should look forward to here.

There’s also the Memory Growth Bonus, another limited-time event that you can take advantage of to grow your Memories. The even bigger news is that you can target your Wishes through the Xspace Echo, which lets you select five Memories to create your own pool from. You can use this to get any Memories you might not have, of course.

On the topic of Memories, you’ll also be able to unlock new second anniversary KV Memories, as part of a Yearly Highlights Event that will let you look back on your own journey with the game over the past year.

On the story and narrative side, Throne of Eros adds two new main stories, with new branches for Xavier, and Rafayel. There’s even a narrative-specific event that will run throughout the anniversary period, through which you can earn two daily outfits for each of the five love interests.

The celebrations also extend to new anniversary content like mail, and video calls. You can purchase a Yearly Pass, and check out some new arrivals at the Lunar Shop.

Beyond the anniversary content, version 5.0 also adds a new feature to the game: Home, which essentially offers a hub to get you directly to interacting with love interests that doesn’t have to do with combat or story.

You can also expect various other quality of life updates that touch on the Journal, Phone Moments Search, Resources Quick Cleanup, and new Tete-a-Tete that should make interacting with all of them more streamlined.

While this is a special banner, you should brush up on how banners work in Love and Deepspace if you’re unfamiliar. As always, it’s never not a good idea to check our Love and Deepspace codes page for some freebies.

#4223. A.O.T 3 Final Preview: Possibly Shaping Up To Be One of the Best Anime Adaptation Video Games

This is DualShockers' preview of Attack on Titan 3, the penultimate entry in the AOT Video Game series developed by Omega Force and published by Koei Tecmo.

The Attack on Titan series by Hajime Isayama is genuinely one of the most important works for fans worldwide. The show has sparked a massive debate over its controversial ending, but putting that aside, you can’t argue with its overall impact: brilliant storytelling and action that fans will remember for ages.

DualShockers played A.O.T. 3 at a preview event, slashing Titans and humans alike, with the entirety of Attack on Titan's story being adapted.

And now, eight years after the last game in the franchise, Koei Tecmo’s Omega Force is back with Attack on Titan 3. The full game launches next month in December on the PS5, Xbox Series X and S, PC, and Nintendo Switch 2. At DualShockers, we had the opportunity to check out a final preview build, and I must say, as a veteran fan of both the series and the games, they’re truly going out swinging on this one.

One of the biggest changes in Attack on Titan 3 is how it approaches its storytelling. You see, back then there was this evident problem that Omega Force could only adapt parts of the story since the anime was still airing, which meant that you weren’t going to get the full package, or at least, where the manga had reached in contrast to the show.

With AOT3, it still remains true to the storytelling presentation of the prior entries. But rather than simply allowing you to relive the anime's biggest moments through the familiar cast, this game once again introduces an original character for you to create and customize.

Our OC character suffers a devastating loss after their previous squad is wiped out during a Titan encounter beyond the walls. So, after developing a fear of Titans from the incident, they're removed from active duty and assigned to instruct the 104th Cadet Corps. This gives you a chance to interact with familiar faces such as Eren, Armin, and Mikasa before eventually graduating from the instructor role and taking command of your own reconnaissance squad.

This approach is very promising because it gives Omega Force a chance to explore parts of the Attack on Titan universe that don't necessarily receive the same attention in the anime. You're not another member of Eren's generation experiencing everything alongside him. But instead, you're an experienced soldier watching these young cadets grow into the people who will eventually shape humanity's fate.

There are also original story events and character interactions designed to expand on the relationships between your character and the existing cast, which is a very nice gesture for us longtime fans if we want something new from this whole experience, especially for characters that didn’t get a ton of screen time in the main show or earlier seasons.

DualShockers spoke to A.O.T. 3 producer Hideo Suzuki about the new Titans, balancing grittiness with arcade action, and why there's no romance.

Of course, none of this hard work over the past 8 years would matter nearly as much without the one thing that makes AOT such an exciting property to adapt into a video game: its combat.

Fortunately, Omega Force hasn't simply brought back the same Omni-Directional Mobility (ODM) system from Attack on Titan 2 and called it a day. The studio has made several adjustments to how you can move around the battlefield, giving the familiar grappling mechanics far more flexibility while also adding new layers of strategy to Titan encounters.

Previously, much of the combat revolved around attaching your ODM anchors to a Titan, reeling yourself towards it, and timing your attack to strike its nape. While that foundation remains intact, AOT3 has generally put more emphasis on identifying weaknesses before committing to an attack. The gameplay rhythm now feels more like a hybrid between a strategic action game.

You can now target individual body parts, allowing you to damage limbs, interrupt attacks, and temporarily immobilize Titans before going for the finishing blow. This is especially important because these guys are much more aggressive, with new attack patterns that require you to watch their movements rather than blindly rush toward their weak spots.

One of the biggest changes in Attack on Titan 3 is how it approaches its storytelling.

Other noticeably uplifting additions include the maneuverability upgrades and defensive options. You can attach yourself to certain surfaces to reposition, use boost jumps to gain additional height, and even dive or slide along the ground to avoid incoming attacks, which is very useful when dealing with larger Titans during their one-on-one boss fight encounters where you have to stun them for the one-hit kill from their nape area.

As for defensive mechanics, you can use well-timed dodges and parries to defend against incoming attacks. Combat Arts also add another layer of progression, giving you access to powerful unlockable special attacks as you increase your military rank. It's an ambitious evolution of the combat from the prior entries, one that I’m very excited to experience to a greater extent with the full release.

The overall game’s flow looks extremely ambitious, and what I mean is that the game has three working gears in motion for the full package here: interacting with your squadmates at the base, the main story missions that progress the campaign, and your Exterior missions.

The latter is one of the highlights, as it lets you freely explore the world with your squad in tow to hunt down more Titans and fulfil different requests from NPCs you come across. It’s essentially a way to give you more gameplay freedom instead of railroading you from start to finish to showcase the anime's main story, and doing Exterior missions also lets you reap additional rewards and useful upgrade materials, which you definitely need and can’t skip since they let you enhance your equipment.

And speaking of gameplay freedom, you can put any doubts to rest about whether you can jump into this game without prior experience with how the first two games worked. There are a bunch of accessibility and control scheme options that let any player easily enjoy the story, but if you want total control, you can turn off any options that automate the combat mechanics, which I honestly prefer since you’re way more vulnerable to mistakes that way, and it makes the game more punishing.

Still, I can promise you that Attack on Titan 3 is genuinely worth having on your radar for the December releases. With how much I got to sample here, I can’t wait to see how more of the character interactions play out, how the talent points fully work with everything in place, along with how the noteworthy battles in the show play out here, and that includes the whole sections of Marley from Season 4 and beyond. It is a lot to look forward to on my side, but I’ll gladly march into battle head-on with my goth Scout Corps Captain.

#4222. Cover Reveal – Tomb Raider: Legacy Of Atlantis

Game Informer’s next cover story is Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, the upcoming reimagining of the original 1996 Tomb Raider arriving on February 12. Since that game celebrates the franchise’s 30th anniversary this year, we’re doing the same with a double-whammy of Tomb Raider features.

We visited Crystal Dynamics’ office to play Legacy of Atlantis for several hours, including an exclusive tour of the Greece section. For our 12-page cover story, we spoke to key team members at Crystal Dynamics and Flying Wild Hog to learn why it’s tackling Lara Croft’s seminal adventure once again (having already remade the game once in Tomb Raider: Anniversary), how this version of the game differs from previous incarnations and why, discuss the teams' controversial use of AI development tools, and how Legacy of Atlantis plants seeds for the upcoming Tomb Raider: Catalyst.

The issue also includes a six-page retrospective of Tomb Raider’s 30-year history, with insights from Crystal Dynamics. This celebration is reflected in our cover art, designed by Tomb Raider franchise art director Brenoch Adams, which showcases every version of Lara Croft from the Core Design, Legend, Survivor, and current eras.

The December issue also marks the return of our annual (and very large) holiday buyers guide, featuring curated gift suggestions for the gamers in your life ahead of the winter holidays. Furthermore, we’ve created a list of family-friendly games to enjoy with younger relatives during upcoming holiday gatherings. Guest contributor Veerender Singh Jubbal writes about India's emerging game development scene and how its community is helping elevate local titles to an international stage. Ahead of the launch of Ryu Ga Gatoku’s Stranger Than Heaven, executive editor Brian Shea played a new section of the era-spanning Yakuza/Like a Dragon prequel while picking the brains of its lead designers for details on the game’s plot, themes, and time periods. Senior associate editor Wesley LeBlanc shares his glowing impressions of Murals, the colorful, fairy-tale-inspired adventure from Disney Illusion Island developer Dlala Studios, whom he spoke with about the game’s conception.

We also have plenty of previews for upcoming games including Final Fantasy VII Revelation, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV, Muramasa: Revenant Blades, Fate/Extra Record, Tiny Metal 2, Mr. Records, and Eternal Anima. We also have reviews for Gears of War: E-Day, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, Control Resonant, Star Wars: Galactic Racer, Silent Hill: Downfall, and many more.

#4221. Genshin Impact Version Luna 4 introduces three new playable characters, including the long-awaited Moon Maiden Columbina

The first major Genshin Impact update in 2026 is almost here, bringing characters we've been waiting a while to play, and more besides.

Genshin Impact’s latest Special Program has spilled all the beans on the game’s next major update, Luna 4. The update, which arrives on January 14, kicks off 2026 with several bits of new content, including some previously-teased characters.

Dubbed Traveler on a Winter's Night, Luna 4 introduces three new playable characters, and brings back The Lantern Rite event to celebrate the beginning of the new year.

The first new arrival in Version Luna 4 is Columbina Hyposelenia, the Moon Maiden. Columbina is a 5-Star Hydro Catalyst wielder. Her kit revolves around supporting the squad via Lunar Reactions. She can trigger coordinated Lunar Reaction DMG, even when she’s off the field.

The Moon Maiden’s special ability, Lunar Domain, further boosts all Lunar Reactions by applying a DMG bonus, including summoning more thundercloud strikes for Lunar-Charged reactions. Columbina is also capable of converting Electro-Charged, Bloom, and Hydro Crystallize reactions into Lunar Reactions, as well as revive fallen squad members.

Speaking of elemental reactions, new in this version is Lunar-Crystallize, a new reaction that’s triggered when Geo meets Hydro (under certain conditions). When triggered, Lunar-Crystallize summons three Moondrifts near enemies. When triggered three times, Moondrift Harmony gets activated, dealing Geo DMG to enemies caught in its radius.

Then there’s Zibai, an Adeptus from Liyue. Zibai is another 5-Star character, a Geo Sword wielder. Zibai can, through entering a special state where they can build up energy, unleash an Elemental Skill that deals Lunar-Crystallize DMG.

The longer the fight goes on, the more Lunar-Crystallize reactions are triggered, the higher (and more often) the damage of Zibai’s Elemental Skill becomes.

Luna 4 continues the Nod-Krai story arc, with a big confrontation with Il Dottore. This is the focus of the new Archon Quest, completing which will earn you a new outfit. There’s a gameplay element to that new chapter, too, with the reveal of Piramida, a new area north of the region. Piramida is the headquarters of the Lightkeepers.

The first phase of Luna 4’s Event Wishes will, unsurprisingly, feature Columbina. It’ll also include reruns of Ineffa. The second phase is when Zibai becomes available, alongside another newcomer: Illuga, a 4-Star, polearm-wielding Geo Lightkeeper. The second phase’s rerun will be Neuvillette, who’s also going to have a new outfit in the shop at a discount.

Version Luna 4 brings back the annual Lantern Rite event, taking place in the mainland of Liyue. The event features its own set of minigames with unique rewards, alongside new stories of the Adepti.

All around Liyue Harbor, you’ll be able to place Xiao Lanterns and inscribe them with messages for others to read. You’ll also earn some Fortune Coins from Auspicious Treasure Trees, which you can later exchange for gifts.

All players will receive 1,600 Primogems through the in-game mail. If you log in regularly, you can earn up to ten Intertwined Fates. Lantern Rite has a new outfit for Yaoyao, which is also where you have a chance to earn one 4-Star Liyue character for free.

Finally, you can look forward to the new Classic Mode in Miliastra Wonderland, which lets you invite select Teyvat characters to join you.

#4220. Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel

Used coffee grounds may be far more valuable than they appear. Instead of ending up in the trash, this everyday waste could provide ingredients for renewable fuels and a variety of useful chemicals. Researchers at Universitat Rovira i Virgili (URV) have identified an efficient way to recover oil from discarded coffee grounds while keeping the remaining material suitable for other industrial applications.

The findings, published in Biomass and Bioenergy, highlight the untapped potential of spent coffee grounds, a waste product generated in enormous quantities worldwide. Global coffee bean production reaches approximately 10 million metric tons annually, but only a small fraction of the beans' material makes its way into the brewed beverage. Much of the rest is discarded as solid waste. These leftover grounds contain roughly 15% lipids, or fats, which can serve as ingredients for producing biodiesel.

Finding a More Efficient Way to Extract Oil From Coffee Grounds

To determine how best to recover these valuable oils, researchers Jorge F. Romero, Alberto Tampieri, Daniel Montané, Magdalena Constantí, and Francesc Medina from URV's Department of Chemical Engineering examined three variables: extraction temperature, processing duration, and the amount of solvent used relative to the coffee grounds.

The team used n-hexane, a solvent widely employed to separate fats from other materials. Through a series of carefully designed experiments, they evaluated how changes in temperature, extraction time, and solvent quantity affected the results, both individually and in combination.

"We have found that the optimal conditions are at 45°C for 60 minutes with a ratio of 35 milliliters of hexane per gram of dry residue," explained Magdalena Constantí, one of the study's authors.

Under these conditions, the researchers recovered approximately 90% as much oil as could be extracted using Soxhlet, a standard laboratory method known for its high extraction yields. Although Soxhlet is effective, it generally takes longer, consumes more energy, and is less practical for large industrial operations.

The newer approach also produced considerably cleaner oil. The optimized extraction yielded just 0.3% impurities, compared with 3.9% using Soxhlet. Chemical analysis revealed that the oil's fatty acid composition remained consistent across the different experimental conditions, with linoleic and palmitic acids making up the largest shares. This composition supports the oil's potential use as an ingredient in biodiesel production.

Coffee Waste Could Produce More Than Just Biodiesel

Recovering oil is only one part of the opportunity. The scientists also wanted to ensure that extracting the fats would not destroy the remaining coffee material, which contains compounds that could be used to manufacture additional fuels and chemicals.

"In our study, we also demonstrate that extracting the oil does not mean that the rest of the material cannot be used for something else," pointed out Francesc Medina, a researcher at the Department of Chemical Engineering who participated in the research.

A central goal was to protect the structural components of the leftover coffee grounds, collectively known as the lignocellulosic matrix. This material contains cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, substances that can be processed into products such as bioethanol, lactic acid, polyhydroxyalkanoates, phenolic compounds, and ingredients used to produce sustainable aviation fuels.

Removing the oil may actually make the remaining material easier to process. Fats can form a barrier that prevents solvents and catalysts from reaching other useful components within the plant matter. By extracting the oils without substantially changing the underlying structure, the researchers created a residue better suited for further processing.

In this way, the method serves two purposes. It recovers a potentially valuable source of biodiesel ingredients while preparing the leftover biomass for conversion into other products.

A Simpler Approach to Sustainable Biofuel Production

The team also investigated whether more advanced extraction methods could deliver better results. These included techniques that use ultrasound or microwaves to accelerate oil recovery.

Although both alternatives can speed up the early stages of extraction, neither offered a sufficiently compelling overall improvement. When the researchers considered oil purity, extraction efficiency, energy requirements, and the potential to expand production to an industrial scale, the conventional batch process using n-hexane under moderate conditions emerged as the more balanced option.

That combination of efficiency and practicality could make the method useful in biorefineries, facilities designed to convert biological materials into fuels, chemicals, and other products.

The research also supports the broader goal of creating a circular economy, in which materials that would otherwise be thrown away are reused to generate additional value. This approach is particularly relevant as industries search for renewable fuel alternatives in sectors that are difficult to electrify, including heavy transportation.

By finding ways to make use of both the extracted oils and the remaining coffee grounds, the scientists hope to reduce waste while expanding the range of materials available for sustainable fuel production.

As Daniel Montané, another researcher involved in the study, explained, the goal is "to transform a typically underused waste product into various energy vectors and bio-based chemical products, and to reduce the environmental impact associated with its accumulation."

The findings suggest that discarded coffee grounds could eventually become an important feedstock for producing renewable fuels and other valuable materials, turning a familiar source of everyday waste into a resource with multiple industrial uses.

Materials provided by Universitat Rovira i Virgili. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4219. 10 Best Soulslikes With Fluid Movement Mechanics

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Soulslikes represent a subgenre of ARPGs with quite distinct characteristics, including various constraints intended to establish their aggressive and challenging nature.

Features such as combat that prioritize functionality over spectacle, as well as limited and mundane traversal methods, are a constant among Soulsborne games' descendants, precisely because they exploit these limitations to create immersive experiences.

It's an incredibly delicate balance because, if poorly executed, it leads to clunky campaigns where the mere act of moving from one place to another can become tedious, though there are also exceptions that prove the rule.

Therefore, in order to shed light on these anomalies and draw on the contributions of titles with a lighter approach to the genre, here are the ten best Soulslikes with fluid movement mechanics.

Since I first played it, I think I've been one of Elden Ring Nightreign's most fervent critics, as it's a title that constantly contradicts me to the point of including it in a list of Soulslikes despite being developed by FromSoftware.

However, if there's one thing I not only can't complain about, but which I sincerely find masterful within the genre, it's the way it agilizes movement to a maximum. It gives each playthrough a dynamism uncommon in the genre.

Thanks to the characters' speed, their ability to climb walls, the spirit streams to jump to incredible heights, and the Spectral Hawk flight, which allows you to hover over areas with remarkable accuracy regarding your landing spot, simply wandering around is quite satisfying—a statement I can't make about almost any other title of this kind.

Is it cheating to include a game from the original influences' roots, which is also more of a roguelite, in this list? Perhaps, yet this is the first time the study has taken movement so seriously, so it deserves the mention.

Phantom Blade Zero is a fusion of traditional action-adventure elements with ideas borrowed from both Soulslikes and Metroidvanias, creating an extravagant yet highly satisfying cocktail.

The game boasts a staggering array of flashy weapons whose visual grandeur is breathtaking, especially in the hands of an ultra-powerful protagonist who is capable of putting those tools at the movement's mercy.

With the ability to sprint at high speed, swing on chains to cross gaps, run along walls, and use a grappling hook to reach high points, this title refuses to simply block doors on one side but instead strives to add depth to the exploration.

Unfortunately, most of these mechanics are prompts that can only be activated at specific, controlled locations, but they are more than enough to make Phantom Blade Zero a more dynamic game than average in this regard.

If you’re looking for the best FromSoftware-inspired ARPGs, I recommend the best Soulslikes based on critics' scores.

Speaking of middle ground, Nine Sols takes Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice's combat system and Hollow Knight's perspective, platforming, and exploration to create one of the decade's most wonderful indie games.

While it leans towards one or the other inspiration depending on the context, it's incredible how Yi soars across the maps once you've unlocked all of his movement tools, which are simple in concept but incredibly rewarding in execution.

Surely, it's nothing more than double jumps, dashes, and kicking enemies' skulls to get airborne, but it's enough to perfectly complement his prodigious combat mechanics.

Even if Nine Sols had terrible traversal, it would still be great because of how it shines in all the other elements, making the polished movement mechanics all the more admirable.

Especially considering it was released when Soulslikes were still in their infancy, Salt and Sanctuary was a major surprise, perfectly adapting the genre's formula to the 2D side-scrolling perspective.

With a wealth of secrets hidden behind the movement abilities you progressively unlock, it's a title that knows how to make platforming satisfying and imbue it with meaning beyond simply moving from point A to point B.

When you first change the gravity orientation, for example, you realize Salt and Sanctuary isn't just a great action RPG with challenging bosses and outstanding worldbuilding, but a game that understood that part of the Dark Souls trilogy's charm lay in how it transformed each new tool into a way to reinterpret the levels.

Years have passed, and I still believe it's the purest and most outstanding 2D Soulslike among those that don't venture too far into other genres, as few have captured the essence of their inspiration as well as this one.

Team Ninja is among the developers that have placed the most emphasis on the Soulslike genre, and while Rise of the Ronin isn't their most outstanding iteration, it certainly stands out when movement is the key factor.

Based on its open-world concept, the game boasts one of the most inventive arrays of traversal tools the genre has ever seen, offering a horse, a grappling hook, and a glider to facilitate the discovery of its expansive map.

If you compare it to direct peers like Ghost of Tsushima, it might fall short, but if the conversation turns to previous titles from the studio, such as Nioh, or games from FromSoftware, like the aforementioned Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, the tone shifts.

Ultimately, Rise of the Ronin combines a myriad of ideas that will appeal to some and deter others, though the fact that it brings with it a form of exploration that avoids relying solely on walking and fast travel is undeniable.

If you’re still waiting for the next FromSoftware game, check out these ten Soulslikes that most people haven’t played but definitely should.

Shattered - Tale of the Forgotten King is a fascinating title due to its attempt, although often erratic, to combine 3D combat with side-scrolling platforming, which is a unique approach even outside Soulslikes' spaces.

The combat is present and functional enough to sustain the experience for the hours it lasts, yet what truly catches the eye is the movement, as it feels like Journey thanks to its flow and smoothness.

In addition to its perspective shifts, which alternate between combat and 2.5D traversal, moving through its open world on a hoverboard feels compelling, mainly because of how unexpected it is to encounter such a mechanic in this type of game.

Indeed, there isn't much to do once you're in free-roaming areas, but since this article focuses on movement mechanics, Shattered - Tale of the Forgotten King keeps its place among the most distinguished in the genre.

While the first game in the series was pure action-adventure, and the second shifted towards open-world RPG elements, Darksiders 3 changed course once again, this time aiming to be both a Soulslike and a Metroidvania.

By merging the level design and combat system of the former with the progression and backtracking mechanics of the latter, Gunfire Games created a phenomenal symphony that truly draws on its hack-and-slash heritage.

Darksiders 3 embraces grandeur, allowing you to transform into diverse avatars to double jump and burn through barriers, glide on air currents, become an energy ball to cling to walls, or even walk on water.

If you add to all these different ways of traversing the use of Fury's whip to swing from platform to platform, the only logical conclusion left to draw is that Darksiders 3 is a marvel when it comes to moving around.

Another Crab's Treasure is among the most creatively designed Soulslikes we've had the pleasure of enjoying this decade, and its movement mechanics are anything but an exception.

The game's levels are extremely vertical and branching, so it needed movement methods that could handle its demanding platforming sections with jumps, climbs, glides, and directional grappling hooks that take you from one ledge to another in a matter of seconds.

It's no wonder the game has become a favorite among speedrunners; its open areas combined with its fluid maneuverability create the perfect breeding ground for exploring the limits of gravity and Krill's stamina.

It has incredible bosses, extensive customization, a remarkable audiovisual component, strong thematic cohesion... Another Crab's Treasure is a complete package, and thankfully, Aggro Crab didn't leave platforming out of the equation.

If you're looking for community-endorsed experiences, I recommend you try these ten Soulslikes where the user score is higher than the critic score.

After Hollow Knight established the Soulslite variant as an alternative for those who didn't want to fully commit to the formula, Hollow Knight: Silksong further solidified its fresh take on the genre.

The loss of resources upon death, save points that also serve as locations to modify your character, pattern-based bosses, cryptic lore... We all know the points of convergence, but where it truly breaks away is in its movement.

Even when compared to pure platformers, Hollow Knight: Silksong possesses a unique grace when it comes to traversal, with an incredibly agile Hornet who's capable of using her abilities in unique ways to facilitate her journey through Pharloom.

Grabbing ledges, bouncing off environmental elements, flying on air currents, leaping between walls, using your needle to propel yourself forward... The array of abilities available during the game is incredible and, above all, very satisfying, especially when you learn to chain them together and run without anything or anyone stopping you.

Nevertheless, beyond the games made by FromSoftware itself or titles that only tangentially touch on the genre, the purest example of a Soulslike with the most fluid movement mechanics is Valor Mortis.

Coming from Ghostrunner, One More Level leveraged its undeniable aptitude for first-person platforming and created an entire world around it, giving us an adventure where you jump, dash, swoop, and grapple with impressive ease.

Valor Mortis is already a striking project for its combination of such divergent concepts as stealth, first-person shooting, and ARPG combat based on parries, though adding such natural platforming sections on top of all that is simply incredible.

I spent the entire campaign amazed by the simple fact that Soulslikes don't move this fast and seamlessly, much less in sequences where you're speeding around in a minecart or running across platforms that are collapsing because a giant monster is attacking you with its tentacles.

Valor Mortis is a game that can be criticized for many things, but not for its movement. In fact, this is an area where it excels so much that other games should strive to emulate its talent.

From the indie ecosystem to productions approaching AAA measures, these are ten Soulslike franchises that should come back by 2027.

#4218. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

Void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”

The game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

Boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

Between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

The rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research new mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

#4217. Heartopia captures the hearts of Animal Crossing and The Sims fans to become the No.1 free download across 50 countries

Heartopia is officially the first big mobile launch of 2026, as the game grabs the attention of millions worldwide.

Heartopia, the new cosy life sim from XD Games, has officially arrived on mobile, right on schedule. If you’ve been keeping up with Heartopia news, you’re likely already aware that the game has pushed back its Steam release to an indeterminate point in 2026.

Doesn’t look like it mattered much, however, as this has already been a big launch on iOS and Android — it probably helps that PC players aren't being entirely left out of the fun, since the game is already available there via XD's own cross-device platform TapTap.

XD Games announced today that Heartopia has reached the top spot on the App Store’s downloads page for free games, and it managed to do so in more than 50 countries and regions worldwide.

The developer is celebratig by offering players a lot of free stuff. If you're feeling lucky, you’ll find new outfits and furniture in three gacha banners (Gilded Acorn Exhibitions): Polar Hymn, The Frostguard, and Coolplayism.

XD Games says you can expect regular updates to add more content, through Fashionwaves and Festivals. In fact, the first season - Winter Frost - is already penciled in for sometime in late January, and it’s going to add appropriately wintery activities like ice skating and snowman-building.

In February, a My Little Pony collaboration event will kick off, bringing new inspired outfits, and vehicles to the game.

Heartopia is a clever mix of Animal Crossing, and The Sims. It’s a free-to-play life sim where you can create your own character, dress them up, build a home for them (and decorate it), and go about town visiting and playing with other players’ characters.

The game’s main feature is the ability to take on a hobby, and seven of those are available at launch. You can dig deep into each hobby, either alone or with others, and there’s a progression track dedicated to each one.

Whether you’re among the millions who downloaded the game already, or you intend to so soon, we’ve got a set of helpful guides to get you started. You should check out how to unlock and upgrade hobbies in Heartopia first, before you get deep into finding all cooking recipes. And, of course, this wouldn’t be a big game launch without a bunch of Heartopia codes for some free stuff.

#4216. A new fiber supplement could help millions suffering from irritable bowel syndrome

A specially designed fiber supplement may offer a promising new way to improve gut health for millions of people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Researchers at Edith Cowan University (ECU) have developed and tested a fiber combination that supports beneficial gut bacteria without making common digestive symptoms worse.

The research team at ECU's Nutrition and Health Innovation Research Institute (NHIRI) found that the supplement, called ur gut®, improved gut health in people with IBS without increasing abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation.

IBS affects people around the world, including nearly 11 percent of Australians. Although its exact cause remains unclear, stress, infections, and certain medications may contribute to the condition. Symptoms can also become worse because of particular foods, inadequate sleep, psychological stress, hormonal changes, and lifestyle factors.

Why Common IBS Diets Can Affect Gut Health

People with IBS are frequently advised to follow a low-FODMAP diet, which limits certain carbohydrates that are easily fermented by gut bacteria. Although this approach can help control uncomfortable symptoms, restricting these foods may also have unintended consequences for the gut microbiome.

"For years we've known that a diet low in Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monesaccharides and Polyols (FODMAPs) can relieve symptoms, but they can also reduce beneficial gut bacteria and negatively impact fiber intake over time," lead author Dr. Tina Yan said.

"We wanted to find a way to build better gut health while following a low-FODMAP diet."

The new findings suggest that a carefully formulated fiber supplement could help address this problem, allowing people with IBS to support a healthier gut microbiome while continuing to manage their symptoms through dietary changes.

The researchers attribute the supplement's promising effects to its combination of two ingredients: resistant starch and psyllium husk.

Psyllium appears to slow the breakdown of resistant starch by gut bacteria, allowing more of it to reach deeper sections of the colon before fermentation occurs. This process may increase the production of beneficial compounds that support intestinal health.

Ordinarily, fermentable fiber can be challenging for people with IBS because bacterial fermentation can produce excess gas and increase digestive discomfort. The new formulation appears to offer a way to obtain the benefits of fermentation without aggravating these symptoms.

"Traditionally, fermentable fibers can be difficult for people with IBS because they can increase gas production and discomfort," Dr. Yan said.

"What's exciting about this study is that participants maintained stable symptoms while showing meaningful improvements in their gut microbiota as well as in their gut-related anxiety."

Significant Changes in Gut Bacteria and Anxiety

The researchers observed substantial shifts in the composition of participants' gut bacteria during the intervention. These changes were particularly notable because they occurred over a relatively short period.

"Changes of this magnitude are rarely seen with such a short intervention," ur gut® co-creator Professor Amanda Devine said.

"The study demonstrated that our targeted dietary fiber blend positively reshaped the gut microbiome in people with IBS following a low-FODMAP diet, supporting beneficial bacteria linked to gut and mental health. This was great to see."

Alongside improvements in gut bacteria, participants also experienced reductions in gut-related anxiety. These findings suggest that the supplement's potential benefits may extend beyond changes in the digestive system, although further research will be needed to establish its broader effects.

A New Approach to Managing Irritable Bowel Syndrome

The researchers believe their findings could help shift IBS care toward improving the underlying health of the gut rather than focusing exclusively on avoiding foods that cause discomfort.

"For many people with IBS, success has traditionally meant simply avoiding certain foods," ur gut® co-creator Associate Professor Claus Christophersen said.

"Our findings suggest we may also be able to actively rebuild gut health and the microbiome while not making IBS symptoms worse. That's an important step forward."

By demonstrating that beneficial gut bacteria can be supported without increasing IBS symptoms, the study points toward new dietary strategies that could complement existing treatments.

The ur gut® supplement is already available for purchase. The research team has also created a cookbook featuring recipes designed to help people incorporate the supplement into a healthy diet.

The study, "Dietary fibre blend improves gut health in patients with irritable bowel syndrome following a low FODMAP diet: a randomised, double-blind control trial," was published online in the European Journal of Nutrition.

#4215. PlayStation Adds Major Feature to Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, ARC Raiders, and More

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

A big component of what makes the PS5 an attractive console, besides just being able to play particular games you can’t play elsewhere, is the console’s various built-in graphical perks. Since the PS5 first launched in 2020, its hardware power has remained one of its definitive perks, with the PS5 Pro in particular taking matters further with the inclusion of PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution, better known as PSSR.

In this list, we discuss some of the best PS4 games to play with the PS5 Pro's Image Quality Enhancements option.

Even though the PS5 already has a few years under its belt, the brand isn’t just resting on its proverbial laurels and letting its existing hardware carry it. New advancements in graphical technology are coming out all the time, and even games that looked pretty stunning when they first dropped like Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 can always look a little bit better.

To that end, PlayStation has added support for one of its up-and-coming graphical frameworks, Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), to several more games in the PS5’s library following its initial launch last month exclusively in Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yotei. The newly-upscaled games include Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, Control Resonant, ARC Raiders, The Finals, No Man’s Sky, and Hell Let Loose: Vietnam.

In case you forgot, QSSR is a proprietary AI upscaling framework created in tandem between PlayStation and AMD. This framework came about from Project Amethyst, an ongoing developmental effort between both companies that also gave rise to PSSR. According to the official announcement of the newly-upscaled games on the official PlayStation news blog, QSSR provides “sharper details, cleaner edges, and more stable images than traditional upscalers,” and since it’s built on the same platform as PSSR, it’s easy for games that already use that framework to incorporate it.

QSSR is a proprietary AI upscaling framework created in tandem between PlayStation and AMD.

In that news post, PlayStation got quotes from all of the improved games’ developers on how QSSR has affected their respective titles. Insomniac Games’ Mike Fitzgerald said that, after incorporating the tech into the launch of Marvel’s Wolverine, the studio decided to go back and add it to Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 as well. “We’re excited for players to swing back into our 2023 title and see QSSR’s exciting image stability and sharpness benefits in both Fidelity and Performance modes,” he said.

Sony has introduced a brand-new AI-powered upscaling technology called Quick Spectral Super Resolution.

Remedy Entertainment’s Erik Jansson said that “QSSR gives Control Resonant a much more stable and detailed image, and we’ve worked closely with Sony to have it ready in an update coming in December.”

Embark Studios’ Mikael Linderholm said that QSSR support will be coming soon to ARC Raiders and The Finals, and said that his studio is “very happy to see Sony’s continued investment in PlayStation technology translate into meaningful improvements for all players.”

While I’m personally of the belief that graphics alone don’t automatically make a game good, it is still pretty interesting to see the degree to which graphical fidelity can be improved, especially as we start to run up against the proverbial limits of realism.

Obviously, the use of AI in games is a feisty topic, particularly in presentation elements like voice acting. In the specific use case of graphics, some efforts like NVIDIA’s AI-powered DLSS5 and its widely-mocked “yassify filter” on character models is probably not the optimal way to be going about this. Rather than trying to generate and overwrite existing graphics with slop, something like QSSR is closer to the ideal, taking what’s already present and merely smoothing out the rougher edges of the environmental rendering process.

PlayStation has promised that this tech will be coming to more games, ending its news post by saying, “Developers are just getting started, and we’re excited to keep working with them to bring QSSR to more games on PS5 in the coming months.”

Two classic apocalyptic shooters have received free modern graphical facelifts.

#4214. Diablo 4's long-awaited Tower and its Leaderboards enter beta today, and there's no PTR funny business this time

Diablo 4's first big moment of 2026 is nearly upon us, and it's one feature many have been looking forward to for actual years.

Diablo 4 is about to deliver on Blizzard’s years-old promise to add a challenging, leaderboard-driven experience to the action RPG. The beta for The Tower, and its associated Leaderboards are about to kick off.

As recently revealed, the new experience launches today at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT. This is a beta version that arrives alongside update 2.5.2.

This early launch won’t offer the full experience, and it’s mainly designed to get it into the hands of players early so that Blizzard could get as much feedback as possible and incorporate it into the final version.

The beta is available to everyone, which is a nice change from the usual rigmarole players would have to go through to get the PTR build and play on a different branch. The Tower, and Leaderboards will be available only in the Seasonal Realm, however. Indeed, the plan is to build on what’s there with each future season, so it’s best to think of it as a seasonal experience.

The Tower is about as simple of an activity as you can get in an action RPG. The goal is to climb as many floors as you can as quickly as you can, all while battling increasingly difficult mobs.

You need to reach and beat the Tower’s final boss before you can call it a run. The Leaderboard will then show your time, and let you see how well you did compared to other players.

The Tower is available to anyone who completed Rank 2 of the current Season Rank. Once done, an Obelisk will appear in Cerrigar, letting you access the challenge.

The Leaderboards themselves will operate on a two-week schedule, all of which will take place during a given season. In this case, they’re going to close the day before Season of the Divine Interversion - the game’s current season - ends.

Blizzard published an updated set of patch notes that show how much has changed since The Tower, and Leaderboards first became playable in the patch 2.5.0 PTR.

Though the two new additions have been anticipated for a while, there’s not been much exciting going on in the world of Diablo 4, apart, of course, from the surprise arrival of The Paladin class, which became available in December last year to coincide with the announcement of Lord of Hatred, the game’s next expansion.
