#4191. 10 Great Games That Defined The Original Xbox

Eric Warner is a Journalist and Multimedia Producer based in New England with over 7 years of experience producing stories for multiple publications

25 years ago, on November 15th, 2001, the gaming industry was forever changed when Microsoft officially dived into the console gaming market with the debut of its first home console, simply called the Xbox.

Designed to be a bridge between the hardware and software capabilities of PCs and the accessibility of home gaming consoles, the original Xbox console took the world by storm with its revolutionary gaming titles and services, proving that the United States can still rival Japanese gaming prospects.

With the original Xbox, and the overall Xbox brand, celebrating its momentous 25th anniversary this November, here’s a look back at 10 great exclusive games that defined the original Xbox and helped pave the way for Microsoft to become a modern gaming juggernaut.

Today, Xbox is largely known for three exclusive franchises: Halo, Gears of War, and Forza but long before the latter simulation racing series took the Xbox brand by storm during the Xbox 360 era, there was another series that stood as Xbox’s premier exclusive racing franchise: Project Gotham Racing.

Originally released as one of the Xbox’s many launch titles, the first Project Gotham Racing allowed up to four players in split-screen multiplayer to race against each other using 29 of the hottest cars of the early 21st century across San Francisco, London, Tokyo, and New York City.

With its stunt-focused Kudos point system and fun, arcade-like modes, Project Gotham Racing became one of the earliest Platinum Hits on the Xbox, leading to the development of three direct sequels, a few spinoffs, and the hit Xbox Live Arcade game, Geometry Wars.

Every great console needs its own standout amusing party game, and while Nintendo had Mario Party and PlayStation had Crash Bash, Xbox got its own distinct party game in the form of Fuzion Frenzy.

Another Xbox launch title, Fuzion Frenzy was an original party game not based on any prior IP, with the game being set in a futuristic tournament pitting four players against one another across randomized or pre-selected minigames with the goal of obtaining as many orbs and points as possible.

Chaotic minigames like Paint Panic and Falling Star quickly made Fuzion Frenzy a fan-favorite, and while it only got one sequel on the Xbox 360, many players still go back to play its wacky games to this very day (thanks to FF being backwards compatible on every future Xbox platform).

The sixth generation of consoles was a time for beginnings and a time for endings for many in the gaming industry at the time, most notably Sega. The Sega Dreamcast would mark the end for its home console prospects.

However, the failure of the Dreamcast didn’t mark the end for several Sega properties, as Microsoft collaborated with Sega to make the Xbox the exclusive home for several Dreamcast ports and sequels. Arguably the best was the funky Jet Set Radio Future.

A sequel to Jet Grind Radio, Jet Set Radio Future is a hyper stylized action game set in a futuristic Tokyo, where a group of teenagers called the GGs skate throughout the city and spray paint graffiti as a form of resistance against the dominating Rokkaku Group megacorporation.

Fans of the original Xbox who want play adventure titles that feature villains as protagonists should check out these 10 games

The RPG giant that is Bethesda is currently owned by Microsoft, and is a major part of Xbox’s future game investments. The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel is rumored to become a Project Helix exclusive, but long before Microsoft purchased Bethesda, the two companies first collaborated to release The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind exclusively on the original Xbox.

The first Elder Scrolls title to debut on a home console, The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind was a first and third-person RPG set in the titular ash-clouded Tamriel province of Morrowind, following a customizable prisoner who sets out on a journey to defeat the oppressive Dagoth Ur.

While Morrowind hasn’t aged as well as its successors, it paved the way for Bethesda to debut other landmark RPGs, such as Fallout, Skyrim, and Starfield on consoles, helping showcase the immense potential of western RPGs.

One of the greatest innovations the original Xbox featured was the creation of Xbox Live, as it was one of the first online multiplayer gaming services designed for home consoles and practically laid the groundwork for all modern online gaming services. Xbox Live’s debut title was MechAssault.

Set in the multimedia BattleTech franchise, MechAssault is a third-person mech shooter game set on the planet Helios. It follows a Wolf's Dragoons BattleMech pilot as they attempt to liberate the planet from the technology-worshipping faction Word of Blake.

MechAssault’s campaign is a lot of fun, but the game is far more famous for its multiplayer as it was one of the first console titles to feature Quick Matches, the ability to host and invite friends to online games, and multiplayer DLC such as new maps, gametypes, and new types of mechs like Raven and Loki.

Every sixth generation console featured fantastic titles that were beloved by many but just didn’t sell well enough to receive proper sequels, resulting in these types of games becoming cult classics. There’s no better Xbox cult classic out there than Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge.

Loosely based on the 1998 Crimson Skies board game, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge has players embody Fortune Hunters air pirate gang leader Nathan Zachary, in an alternate 20th century where planes and zeppelins became the primary mode of transportation and the U.S. split into warring nations.

With an interesting world and story highly reminiscent of classic pulp books and films like Indiana Jones and enthralling third-person fighter plane gameplay, Revenge quickly became a fan-favorite. While it never received a sequel, it has since become the unofficial mascot for Xbox’s backwards compatibility.

These classic games will require some work to play again unless you have an older-gen console.

Early on in the Xbox brand’s history, Xbox’s most famous exclusive franchises were Halo, Gears of War, and Peter Molyneux's highly ambitious fantasy RPG Fable, which is finally set to return to Xbox early next year with a reboot of the series.

The original Fable was claimed by Molyneux to be the most ambitious RPG of the sixth console generation, with the game supposedly allowing players to have children in-game, play through the protagonist’s entire life, and witness plant life grow throughout the game, among other promises.

While most of these features weren’t present in the first Fable game, the original Fable still turned out to be an incredibly charming, comedic, and overall fun RPG, thanks to its witty British humor, morality system, and vast numbers of ways to interact with NPCs such as getting married and farting on people.

Nintendo fans recently got to take part in the midnight launch of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake launch at various gaming stores. Those launch events paled in comparison to the cultural phenomenon that was the launch of Halo 2.

The original Xbox was arguably the house Halo: Combat Evolved built, and as such, most gamers in the world were excited to see how Bungie would improve upon the series in Halo 2, leading to the sequel receiving 1.5 million U.S. pre-orders and selling over 2.4 million copies in its launch day alone.

This anticipation was warranted though, as Halo 2 became the most popular Xbox Live game up until the release of Gears of War 1 and is widely regarded to feature one of the best FPS campaigns of all time thanks to the introduction of the Arbiter, dual-wielding, vehicle hijacking, and more.

The original Xbox was home to very few JRPGs, but these obscure ones might have something left exploring if you're interested.

While Fable 1 is the RPG most associated with the original Xbox, I would argue that it wasn’t the best RPG available on the console, with that honor instead going to BioWare’s epic 2003 masterpiece Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic.

Many Star Wars video games were released exclusively for the original Xbox, but KOTOR was by far the most notable. It not only took place roughly 4,000 years before the events of the films during the Jedi Civil War, but featured one of the greatest gaming twists of all time, centered around Darth Revan.

KOTOR’s rather clunky round-based combat hasn't exactly aged well over the years, but its story and characters are still regarded as being some of the best to appear any RPG, such as Darth Malak, Jedi Knight Bastila Shan, the murderous droid HK-47, and the Mandalorian Canderous Ordo to name a few.

Finally, without a doubt, the number one exclusive video game that defined the original Xbox and arguably the Xbox brand overall was the launch title and Bungie’s revolutionary FPS Halo: Combat Evolved.

Halo: Combat Evolved was the definitive console-based FPS that truly showcased the capability of consoles to deliver an engaging, fun, and wondrous FPS experience, thanks to its cinematic quality, wide-open spaces, addictive gunplay and vehicle combat, and engrossing FPS multiplayer maps.

If Halo: Combat Evolved hadn’t been packaged with most Xbox consoles on day one, Xbox likely wouldn’t have lasted beyond the sixth generation of consoles and CE’s success ultimately led to Xbox not only obtaining a mascot with Master Chief but the creation of one of the most beloved sci-fi multimedia franchises of all time.

To celebrate Gears of War: E-Day's release and Gears' upcoming 20th anniversary, here's a ranking of every campaign in the Gears of War franchise.

#4190. The Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Easter Eggs That Did And Did Not Make It Into The 2026 Remake

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is a game full of Easter Eggs, secrets, and hidden mechanics (did you know if a butterfly lands on your Deku Stick, it summons a fairy?). Now in its second remake, not every secret has made its way forward through the previous iterations, but many have. Below you will learn about a few of the secrets that made the cut, and others that didn’t.

In the courtyard where Link first meets Zelda, there is arguably the most fourth-wall-breaking Easter Egg in the whole game. If you don’t rush to Zelda and instead pause and enter first-person to look around, you will see portraits of other Nintendo characters through the windows, like Mario and Yoshi. In the 3DS remake, the portraits are replaced by an image of a Mario stage.

For the 2026 remake, there are no references to other Nintendo characters. Instead, the tapestry you build over the course of the game is on display. Removing the reference to Nintendo characters outside of the Zelda universe is understandable, but it is a little odd that art representing the full adventure of the game – an adventure that has not yet concluded – is on the wall.

As stated above, the Nintendo character portraits are gone, but there is still a guard you can annoy. If you fire a Deku Seed into the left window, a guard will pop out, yell at you, and then throw a bomb at you. You can’t pick up the bomb. In fact, at this point in the game, you haven’t even seen a bomb.

The Hyrule Castle portrait references to Yoshi and Mario are gone (though Mario and Luigi are still kind of in the game in a way), but Bowser gets a pass for some reason. Both Malon and her dad, Talon, are still wearing Bowser pins on their clothes. And unlike the N64 game where the detail was a little vague, there is no mistaking it here.

Gossip Stones are all over Ocarina of Time and it takes a while to understand what they do. If you hit them with a sword, they tell you the time, and if you play Zelda’s Lullaby near them, they refill your magic. If you do the Happy Mask Salesman’s side quest, interacting with them while wearing the Mask of Truth offers little hints and details about the world. But then there are interactions that are just odd for no reason. Blowing up a bomb near a Gossip Stone still makes it take off like a rocket ship, and using the Megaton Hammer still flattens them for a moment like a Looney Tunes.

And speaking of playing Zelda’s Lullaby for inanimate objects, if you slash a sign to pieces with your sword and regret your words and deeds, you can play the iconic tune to make the signs reform and become readable again.

This detail was exclusive to the 3DS remake of Ocarina of Time, and surprising no one, it has been removed. Ocarina of Time launched in June 2011 and Nintendo released Skyward Sword about five months later in November. For… marketing purposes, I guess, Skyward Sword art could be found in Lonlon Ranch, the Bombchu Shop in Hyrule Castle Town, and the Gerudo Fortress. It was a fun Easter Egg to discover back in 2011, especially since Skyward Sword was still months away, but these days it’s a bit of an odd inclusion.

Though never explicit, the composer ghosts guarding the Sun’s Song (and Link’s first ReDead encounter) have always been assumed to be inspired by Mario and Luigi. They are brothers; Flat is short, squat, and red; Sharp is lanky and green. They still appear in Ocarina of Time this way, which isn't surprising, since they are important characters you must meet to get a very useful song. Fans have also speculated that Talon and Ingo are Mario and Luigi-inspired for similar reasons, but it’s worth noting that they are not brothers.

In the Spirit Temple there is a large statue of a woman and for reasons that have never been explained, Link could attach his hookshot to her breasts. It served no purpose. It didn’t help solve a puzzle. If anything, it was confusing. But we all tried it and there is no shame in admitting it! That was removed for the 3DS remake, and it remains removed in 2026.

This is a very subtle reference to Wind Waker/Breath of the Wild/Tears of the Kingdom and is potentially the only addition to the remake that looks toward the future of the Zelda franchise. Obviously, plenty of characters in Ocarina later appear in Majora’s Mask (another remake of that is hopefully being considered), but it would be inaccurate to call those intentional Easter Eggs.

However, in Kokiri Forest and in the neighboring Lost Woods, the magical debris floating in the air often resembles a Korok as it would later appear in the series. It makes sense, too, because the Koroks are meant to be what the Kokiri transformed into following The Great Flood.

For more on the Ocarina of Time remake, you can find our review here. You can also find our interview with the game's producers here.

#4189. Tomorrow's Battlefield 6 patch somehow makes jets more useless, improves armor bar visibility in Redsec

The first Battlefield 6 patch of the year is almost here, bringing a smattering of changes, including one that doesn't quite make sense.

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller update. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

#4188. 8 JRPGs With the Most Nominations at The Game Awards

Murillo Zerbinatto is a JRPG enthusiast, writer, and editor. He has played over 300 RPGs during his gaming career, with 90% of them being JRPGs.

The gaming industry is no stranger to award shows. Nowadays, we have countless ceremonies, such as the Golden Joystick Awards, the BAFTA Games Awards, the D.I.C.E. Awards, and more. However, it is hard to deny the massive influence of Geoff Keighley's The Game Awards, whether because of its sheer audience reach, the spectacle, the world-premiere announcements, or the acceptance speeches that become industry touchstones for years to come.

From Nioh to Black Myth: Wukong, these are the seven Soulslikes with the most nominations at The Game Awards.

We're nearing The Game Awards season, so I put together a themed list to celebrate. Rather than just discussing the ceremony itself, why not look back at the JRPGs with the most nominations at The Game Awards? True to my personal branding around here, I went ahead and did just that. It is wild to think that in the past, JRPGs would barely even be considered for major awards, yet here we are. Not only do they regularly rack up nominations today, but a certain JRPG-inspired title even swept the TGAs and currently stands as the most awarded game in the event's history.

Octopath Traveler caught plenty of people by surprise, myself included. Just when we thought Square Enix had left pixel art behind for good, the company proved there is still plenty of room for the visual style while elevating it to new heights with its HD-2D graphical engine. Beyond the visuals, it recaptured the nostalgia of classic Square titles through the core gameplay loop as well.

Octopath Traveler drew heavy inspiration from Final Fantasy VI to weave together the tales of its eight protagonists. That achievement earned the JRPG three nominations: Best Art Direction, Best Score and Music, and Best Role Playing Game, all of which felt entirely fitting. It didn't walk away with a trophy, but earning those nods showed how deeply critics appreciated the experience at the time.

It's not every day a JRPG competes for Game of the Year, so when it does, you know the game is an absolute banger. As far as I am concerned, if Xenoblade Chronicles 3 had taken home the top prize, it would have been completely deserved. To be fair, it lost both Best Role-Playing Game and Game of the Year to Elden Ring, which is entirely understandable, even if I would still hand the trophy to Monolith Soft if we were running Murillo's TGAs.

Losing Best Score to God of War Ragnarök, however? Look, I know Ragnarök features a wonderful composition, but anyone who has played Xenoblade Chronicles 3, or any Xenoblade title for that matter, heck, any modern JRPG, knows that musical composition is the beating heart of the genre. You could play a JRPG where every other element falls flat, and I guarantee the soundtrack would still blow you away. But I digress, and that is just the fanboy in me talking. I am simply thrilled that a JRPG received that much recognition and spotlight back in 2022.

Speaking of Best Score, NieR: Automata nailed that category in the year it competed, and honestly, that was the bare minimum. If they hadn't given the score award to Automata, who else could possibly have taken it? I do know who beat it out for Best Role-Playing Game that year, though, and I will get to that entry soon. NieR: Automata also earned a nomination for Best Narrative, and while it didn't win, I can understand why.

The story was insanely good, touching on deep philosophical and existentialist themes that leave you chewing on their meanings for months. However, its narrative delivery and structure can feel a bit complex for some players. You have to play through the game multiple times to get the full picture, and while I had a blast on every playthrough, some folks might drop off after the first ending and miss everything NieR: Automata truly offers. Plus, I haven't played What Remains of Edith Finch, and since the TGAs are ultimately a competition, it may have offered a tighter narrative experience.

Even before Final Fantasy XVI hit store shelves, it was already sparking heated debate. I have never minded the franchise evolving its formula, though certain corners of the fanbase got irked just hearing that Final Fantasy XVI would lean into full action combat. Regardless of the broader discourse, I loved the game. It moved 3 million copies at launch (even if Square Enix wasn't fully satisfied with the numbers) and walked away with 4 nominations at the 2023 TGAs.

Had Final Fantasy XVI not launched in the exact same year as Baldur's Gate 3, it might easily have swept more categories, including Best Role-Playing Game and Best Performance, because let's face it, Ben Starr as Clive was perfection. The JRPG did take home Best Score and Music with Masayoshi Soken at the helm, a victory that was overwhelmingly deserved. To this day, I still blast either the Phoenix or Bahamut theme at the gym and feel like a Dominant hoisting weights.

From Axiom Verge to Hollow Knight: Silksong, these are the ten Metroidvanias with the most nominations at The Game Awards.

Remember how I mentioned that NieR: Automata lost Best Role-Playing Game and that the outcome was pretty justifiable? Well, it lost to Persona 5, and given that it stands as one of my all-time favorite JRPGs and the best-selling Persona entry ever, I completely understand the decision. Furthermore, in TGA history, Persona 5 was the first JRPG to compete for the main Game of the Year prize. It didn't win because it went up against The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, and really, who can complain about that outcome?

It still secured Best Role Playing Game over NieR: Automata, Divinity: Original Sin II, and Final Fantasy XV, which speaks to what a stacked year 2017 was for RPG fans. If the votes were up to me, Persona 5 would have swept practically every category and called it a night. It is a JRPG through and through, featuring a slow burn, extensive social sim segments, and mountains of dialogue, yet it still shattered niche barriers to reach a massive global audience. May Atlus keep on winning.

Apparently my wishes were granted in record time, because Atlus kept on winning. While Persona 5 earned 4 nominations, Metaphor: ReFantazio racked up 6 nominations and took home 3 major trophies: Best Narrative, Best Art Direction, and Best Role-Playing Game, edging out Square Enix's own Final Fantasy VII Rebirth. That is an extraordinary feat, mind you. Despite Persona's massive growth, Final Fantasy remains a far more recognizable mainstream brand, making it all the more impressive that critics favored Metaphor.

I adore Metaphor, by the way. It was the very first JRPG I covered right after joining the team here at DualShockers, and I fell in love with it immediately. It is stylish, gutting, gripping, challenging, and endlessly engaging. It came dangerously close to dethroning Persona 5 as my favorite Atlus JRPG, falling just a hair short, though not quite yet. I don't know whether Studio Zero plans to release DLC or jump straight into a follow-up, but I will definitely be there on day one and hope to see its successor pull in even more nominations.

Eagle-eyed readers might notice that I left Final Fantasy VII Remake off this list. That entry received 6 nominations, though including it felt slightly redundant since both games competed in nearly the same categories, simply swapping Best Art Direction for Best Audio Design, while Final Fantasy VII Rebirth added a Best Performance for Briana White as Aerith. She ultimately lost to Melina Juergens as Senua, which is tough luck.

Even so, if we look specifically at Japanese-developed JRPGs (as awkward as that phrasing sounds), Final Fantasy VII Rebirth holds the record for the most nominations in TGA history so far. The title earned nods for Best Game Direction, Best Narrative, Best Score and Music (which it won), Best Audio Design, Best Performance, Best Role-Playing Game (losing to Metaphor: ReFantazio), and Game of the Year (losing to Astro Bot). No matter how hard certain corners of the internet try to downplay Rebirth's success, critics worldwide universally acclaimed it, and I cannot wait to see Final Fantasy VII Revelation rack up just as many nominations and plenty of wins.

We are well past debating whether Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 counts as a JRPG, so I will skip the preamble. What I want to highlight here is something everyone who follows the TGAs already knows: Expedition 33 holds the record as the most awarded game in TGA history. That milestone is not only deeply symbolic for the current climate of the gaming industry, where publishers constantly chase infinite exponential profits, but it also proves that simply throwing massive budgets at a project is not the secret to making a great game.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 represents a union of passionate fans, sheer willpower, rich inspiration, and genuine love for art and video games distilled into something tangible, fun, emotional, and lasting. From the very moment I started playing, I could not put the controller down, completely enthralled by the journey of my Expeditioners. As proof of that obsession, I actually earned the world's first platinum trophy for the game, and I am not kidding. Even director Guillaume Broche himself confirmed it to me on LinkedIn. Not trying to gloat, just showing how transcendental my love for this title truly is.

We're not just talking about Grand Theft Auto VI and Ocarina of Time, but up to seven video games that could sweep The Game Awards.

#4186. The Switch 2 Pro Controller Can Make Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Even Better

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time hit Switch 2 today, and, as Kyle Hilliard pointed out in our review, it is pretty excellent. Along with its remarkable visual upgrade, the new Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time adds quality-of-life improvements and modernizes the control scheme. As part of that, Nintendo has added the ability to jump and sprint. While that works well to make the game feel new, I quickly realized it sometimes clashes with another new improvement: a free camera controlled by the right stick. Holding down the sprint button to get through areas as fast as possible can make it tricky to keep the camera where you want it, but thankfully, if you have the Switch 2 Pro Controller, there's an easy fix.

After hours of running around, I was awestruck by the level of detail and updates, but I found myself constantly fighting with the camera, or at the very least, needing to take a strange claw-style grip to be able to direct the camera with the right stick, while holding down the A button to sprint. If you're a casual Switch 2 player, you might not have even noticed the back buttons on the Pro Controller, or you just have no idea what they do. Those buttons can be remapped on a per-game basis and it's a simple process. Everyone has their own preferences, but, for example, for high-mobility shooters, I like remapping one of those to reload and one to jump. I've never felt the need to remap in a Zelda game, but after feeling the need to do so with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, I might do so going forward.

If you, like me, struggle to comfortably steer the new free camera while running through hallways, towns, dungeons, and, yes, Hyrule Field, you might want to consider remapping your controller. As you can see in the above image, the placement of Jump and Dash on the face buttons can make it difficult to simultaneously control the camera and sprint. This isn't typically a problem in most modern games, as clicking the right stick is often a toggle to sprint, but in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2, you need to hold the button.

If you have the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller, copying one button's functionality to the buttons on the back of the controller is simple. All you need to do is hold the Home button on the Switch 2 Pro Controller for a moment until the Switch 2 system menu appears on the right side. Along with Power Options and any Bluetooth audio devices you have available, there is also the option to map GL and GR, the controller's back buttons on the left and right, respectively.

Navigate down the menu to the GL and GR, then select which one you'd like to map. It will ask you which button you want to assign to the one you selected. Everyone can choose whatever makes sense in their own head, but mapping A (Roll and Dash) to GL and X (Jump) to GR made the most sense to me. Now, while I'm using the Switch 2 Pro Controller, I can use my middle finger to hold the GL button to Dash around without removing my thumb from the camera-controlling right stick.

And the best part is that, since you're not removing the functionality of the A or X buttons, you can still use them when it makes sense. For example, A also controls actions like opening up a treasure chest or door, and in my head, that feels like a face-button action, whereas rolling and dashing feel right mapped to the back buttons. The only downside is that, since this functionality is new for Switch 2 Pro Controllers, it isn't available if you're using the Joy-Cons or a Switch 1 Pro Controller. Also, it can make switching over to handheld mode challenging, as you don't have access to the back buttons in that play style.

Even if you don't have the ability to take advantage of this tip, either because you don't own a Switch 2 Pro Controller or because you prefer playing in handheld mode, you should still absolutely play the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. To learn more about the experience and why it's a must-play, head to our review.

#4181. The Best Rainbow Six Game is Getting an Unexpected Sequel

For nearly two decades, Rainbow Six: Vegas has been left in the past while Siege has become the face of the franchise. The two games offer very different experiences, though. Vegas was built around a proper campaign, room-clearing, and a squad that followed your orders. It's been a long time since Rainbow Six offered anything quite like it.

It was a huge disappointment when Ubisoft cancelled each of these games, and they deserve to be revisited at some point in the future.

Now, Insider Gaming reports that Ubisoft has greenlit a new Rainbow Six: Vegas project at Ubisoft Montreal. It's reportedly codenamed Spades, with a third entry considered more likely than a remake. Ubisoft hasn't announced anything yet, but a new Vegas campaign would be a welcome change of pace.

According to the report, Spades is one of three projects recently started at Ubisoft Montreal, including another game said to be linked to Rainbow Six. There's no word on what that other project might be. Spades itself is believed to be in early development, so its setting, features, platforms, and release window remain unknown.

The original Rainbow Six: Vegas arrived in 2006, followed by Vegas 2 in 2008. Both games streamlined some of the more demanding elements of the early Rainbow Six formula, but they didn't abandon squad tactics. Teammates could be ordered into position, stacked at doors, and sent in with different breach commands. The cover-based firefights could get hectic, but there was usually time to think about how to approach the next room.

The squad AI wasn't always up to the task, either. A badly timed move could turn a straightforward room-clearing attempt into a scramble to keep everyone alive. The teammates weren't terrible, but SWAT 4 generally did a better job with its AI officers. That's one area a sequel could improve without losing the appeal of the older games.

I used to watch Vegas gameplay on a TV show about video games as a kid. I only got around to playing both games years later, and they were well worth it.

I've played most of the Tom Clancy games  over the years, completing and even replaying almost all Ghost Recon and Splinter Cell titles multiple times. Vegas was more linear than some of them, but its mix of tactical gameplay and straightforward action worked particularly well.

The snake cam let you check behind a door before breaching, and different entry points kept encounters interesting. Cover was useful, but the squad commands were what made the firefights memorable. Vegas also placed second in our ranking of the best Tom Clancy games, behind Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory.

Siege has given Rainbow Six a strong multiplayer identity, but there's room for something different alongside it. The older games had campaigns and squad-focused missions that offered a change from competitive multiplayer. A new Vegas wouldn't need to follow the Siege formula. It could bring back a side of Rainbow Six that hasn't had much attention in years.

Siege has given Rainbow Six a strong multiplayer identity, but there's room for something different alongside it.

Rainbow Six Tactics is another welcome development. Turn-based strategy is a good fit for the squad-focused side of the series, and it doesn't need to resemble Vegas to be interesting. A new first-person campaign and a separate tactical strategy game could happily coexist.

As our coverage of Rainbow Six Tactics pointed out, Ubisoft is making it a fully single-player game without an in-game shop or microtransactions. It's currently scheduled for 2027, with Paul Bishop from Vegas 2 returning as the head of Rainbow. That connection is a nice touch, but the turn-based gameplay is interesting in its own right.

If Spades does turn out to be Vegas 3, it has a solid foundation to build on. Keep the squad commands, the room-clearing, and the single-player campaign; make the teammates a little smarter. There isn't much reason to turn it into something else.

The Division 2 is attempting to fuse its ongoing player bases via both Steam and Ubisoft Connect.

#4178. Battlefield 6’s first big map in months is coming to Labs soon, but I'm more excited about BF4's Golmud Railway making its way to BF6

As promised, Battlefield Labs is coming back to bring us a preview of some of Battlefield 6’s upcoming Season 2 content.

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the new maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

Another ambitious online shooter is biting the dust, and this time, it seems that players won't even get the chance to return for one last update.

GFA Games has officially announced today that PIONER, its post-apocalyptic MMO inspired by titles like STALKER and Fallout, is shutting down. The studio is ending development, canceling future updates, and preparing to take the game's servers offline after failing to secure the funding necessary to keep the project running.

In an announcement shared on social media, the development team explained that maintaining PIONER required additional financial support, but they couldn’t find any. The studio had spent the past few months negotiating with existing and potential partners, hoping to find an investment deal that would allow development to continue and preserve the team.

Unfortunately, those discussions didn't lead anywhere. According to the developers, GFA Games no longer has enough money of its own to continue working on the game or maintain its server infrastructure.

After years of near radio silence, Fairgames has been canceled and its staff redistributed throughout Sony games.

“We were unable to agree on the funding needed to continue the project. The studio no longer has sufficient funds of its own to continue development and keep the servers running.”

Aleksandr Nikitin, CEO of GFA Games, even addressed the community, expressing his disappointment over the decision and apologizing to players who purchased PIONER expecting more updates. He explained that the team had envisioned a long future for the project and had been trying to find a way to keep both the game and its developers together.

The recent announcement effectively puts an end to those plans. Since PIONER is an online-only experience, shutting down its servers also means players will no longer be able to access the game once the infrastructure is taken offline.

It's quite an unfortunate outcome for a game that spent years building up expectations before finally arriving on Steam Early Access in December 2025. The post-apocalyptic MMO promised an enormous world filled with dangerous mutants, exploration, survival mechanics, and multiplayer activities, which initially attracted some attention on Steam, reaching a peak of more than 1,600 concurrent players around launch. However, that interest quickly faded. By September, its 24-hour peak had dropped to just 11 players, according to SteamDB.

GFA Games has officially announced today that PIONER, its post-apocalyptic MMO inspired by titles like STALKER and Fallout, is shutting down.

Unfortunately, its launch was plagued by technical issues, and these numbers show that the shooter struggled to maintain a consistent player base in the months that followed. Now, GFA Games revealed that it really was struggling to turn its project into a sustainable live-service experience.

Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble is being shuttered before it could even reach worldwide launch status.

It's always disappointing to see an ambitious multiplayer project disappear like this, especially when players have invested money and time into its world. But the studio thanked everyone who supported PIONER, reported bugs, created content, and helped build its community, while acknowledging that it couldn't deliver the future originally promised.

For now, the development team hasn't provided a specific date for when the servers will go offline. Still, with development and updates officially ending, PIONER's days are numbered. And while the game may not have reached the audience its developers hoped for, its shutdown is another reminder of how difficult it can be to keep an online-only game alive when the players and financial support aren't there.

#4175. Arc Raiders finally reveals early 2026 roadmap, but we’re not getting a new map for a while

The first couple of months of 2026 in the world of Arc Raiders look pretty promising, but the big guns are being held back for now.

After weeks of waiting, Arc Raiders developer Embark has officially unveiled the first few months of the game’s 2026 roadmap. The plan is split into four months, covering January to April, collectively dubbed Escalation.

We’re expecting a content update each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps. There is, however, at least one new map in the works, but it won’t be here until sometime in April.

While we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others. January looks to be the lightest so far, which makes sense given that it’s just a week or so from ending.

January’s chapter is titled Headwinds, kicking off on January 27. This segment will see the addition of a new matchmaking option for players above level 40 - at or near the game’s endgame. We’re also expecting a new Map Condition, and a new Player Project for everyone to contribute to.

Things start getting interesting in February, when Shrouded Sky will begin. This chapter brings three exciting additions to Arc Raiders. There will be a new Map Condition, new Arc Threat, and the start of another Player Project.

Interestingly, we’re going to see some sort of map update during the month, but Embark didn’t share anymore details. The next Raider Deck will also deploy in February, alongside a new Expedition Window.

The Flashpoint chapter begins in March, when we’re expecting another new Map Condition, one more new Arc Threat, as well as another Player Project. March’s most interesting addition is an update to everyone’s trusty rooster friend, Scrappy.

Finally, April is when the big guns come out, because that’s when the first new map of 2026 will arrive in Arc Raiders. With it, comes a new large Arc, which is to be expected. A new Map Condition will debut then, too, likely starting off on the new map.

That’s pretty much it, but seeing as we’re just one day away from the start of the January stage, things are about to get exciting again in Arc Raiders.

#4174. Award-Winning Composer And Musician Jon Batiste Talks Ocarina Of Time's Music And Why 'Guile's Theme' Goes With Everything

Jon Batiste has collaborated with the likes of Alicia Keys, Lenny Kravitz, Prince, Stevie Wonder, Willie Nelson, and many more. He performed the national anthem at Super Bowl LIX. He's headed up the musical efforts of The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. He's taken home more awards than we can realistically list in this article (including eight Grammys, as well as an Academy Award, a BAFTA Award, and a Golden Globe). But as I sit down with Batiste for a brief conversation about video game music, his energy transcends the Zoom call.

Before I can even ask a question, Batiste begins singing to greet me, then nerds out about my NBA Jam and Street Fighter II cabinets. He begins humming the menu music from NBA Jam and reminiscing about all the quarters he pumped into his local Street Fighter cabinet. The Louisiana native and Juilliard School alum has been an ardent gaming enthusiast for nearly three decades, with compositions from games like Sonic the Hedgehog and Final Fantasy VII inspiring his earliest musical endeavors. Spend enough time watching video game music performances on social media, and you'll likely soon find videos of Batiste sitting with famed Final Fantasy composer Nobuo Uematsu, or of Batiste performing gaming music.

With The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time delivering some of the most iconic music of all time (and Batiste famously loving the music), it makes sense that Nintendo would bring him out to New York to serve as a special guest at the launch event for the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2. I sat down with Batiste for a few minutes to chat about his love of video game music, his history with Nintendo, and why "Guile's Theme" from Street Fighter II just goes so well with everything.

Ocarina of Time is easily one of the most important video games ever made, and one of the things that makes it so special is the music. What about Ocarina of Time sticks out to you sonically?First off, if you want to get super inside baseball, technical music nerdery, which I love to do, in the compositions, there's a way that major chords and minor chords in... no sevenths, just root, third, fifth. They alternate, and it creates this magic that is, like, it's wistful, and it's simple. It feels ancient, and it feels like it's the music that is going on in your mind as you're generating thoughts and your imagination is churning. And the major chords are happening just after the minors in this contrary motion that's happening, so it feels like the music is going like this: It's going up – major, minor – like [sings the main Legend of Zelda theme song].

So, it's expanding and contracting, which is a musical allegory for the expansion and the openness of the world that Link is in. It's like [Koji Kondo] figured out how to capture the essence of the gameplay, but also the essence of magic and simplicity, which I think is really what makes... that's the music's power! So, you could listen to the music in the game, and you could also listen to it apart from the game and experience that magic.

Are there any tracks in Ocarina of Time that stand out to you as the most musically sophisticated or compositionally impressive?Oh man. Well, I think of it as a suite, so that's what makes it actually... there's nothing that's more or less complex, but the thought to figure out how to make all of the themes be interrelated yet singular. "Song of Storms" is, like, for me, that's a personal favorite. That's why I like to play it. I like to play a lot of the themes. That's how I grew up! I would play the game, and then, I would go to an instrument. Once we played for hours on Nintendo, we'd go and play Nintendo on piano! It was like a trade-off there, you know? I've been doing this since I was about 11 years old.

Taking it back to that 11-year-old Jon, talk to me a little bit about your history in general.Okay, so my history with Nintendo goes back to the NES. Christmas morning. Duck Hunt. You remember that? Maybe the first game I ever played. No, the first game I ever played was Donkey Kong, and then Duck Hunt, and then Super Mario Bros. Staples! We're talking about the early '90s. We had a room where I would go – it was my domain – and we had this blue shag carpet, and I would sit back there, and I would basically disappear into the carpet playing Nintendo for hours and hours.

And my mind is kind of... my mind can become a spiral; it can become a tornado. And I realized even then that going into this world of the game, even if I didn't win – it's not about winning or losing – it helps to organize the spiral of my mind and give me ideas and inspiration. So then, I started to get into Street Fighter II when I started to play more communally with my sister and my cousins. Yoko Shimomura, who I also had the pleasure of meeting and collaborating with, she composed incredible themes for each character, and that's when I really started to get a true love for fighting games.

And then, we would play so many of the Street Fighter franchise. We would play a lot of Final Fight. There were so many things... there was Double Dragon, then we got Mega Man... all these different series. Mega Man X is [an] all-time favorite. And then, here comes The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and that sort of expands the canon while also blending all of the elements: score, combat, the sort of linear quality of, like, a Donkey Kong or Super Mario World, and expanding the world in that way, expanding the canon in that way. Mind-blowing! So,  that sort of solidified my palate in terms of my favorite type of game.

You mentioned Street Fighter II. There's a meme about "Guile's Theme" and how it goes with everything. What about that composition makes it so it has the ability to enhance whatever video you pair it with?Wow! So, it has momentum in a way that is extremely [sings the melody of "Guile's Theme"] ... It draws you in, which is what you want [with] anything that you're starting when you're commencing a journey or watching something. You want it to draw you in, and that kind of pulls you in as that call and response. But it's an immediate announcement with the brass, and then the bass call and response. So, it's automatically giving you this feeling that something's happening, and I've got to pay attention to it! So that's the first step right there. And the tempo is really... it's a great tempo! It almost has the feeling of the great themes from, like, an '80s protagonist that's in a fighting movie. I think that was kind of the archetype. Yoko was probably drawing from that archetype, right? The action-hero archetype.

#4173. Aurora Gaming sweep Pixel Lumina to reach Europe Qualifier 1 final after BONK disqualification

Aurora Gaming beat Pixel Lumina 2-0 to reach the Europe Qualifier 1 final, days after the UK side that had knocked them out was disqualified for cheating. The final decides seeding for the Europe Qualifier Playoffs, the next step towards VCT EMEA Kickoff 2027 in Berlin.

Aurora Gaming will play in the Europe Qualifier 1 final. Their best-of-three semi-final against Pixel Lumina began at 16:00 on Tuesday. Aurora took the opening map in 41 minutes and closed out the second in 35 minutes.

The win completes a turnaround for a side that had already been eliminated from the qualifier. Their earlier exit had come against BONK.

The fallout reached beyond the bracket. Every BONK player and registered participant was also provisionally suspended, GINX TV reported.

The disqualification forced a rework of the schedule. Riot had set Qualifier 1 for 5 to 8 November as a single-elimination, best-of-three bracket. The Pixel Lumina semi-final and the final were pushed back to make room for the rebuilt bracket. All three affected organisations agreed to the new timetable.

Pixel Lumina, a team based in Hungary, came into the match at rank 120 in the Elo power rankings. They hold a rating of 1559 and a 30-28 record across 58 rated matches. Aurora are unranked. Before this semi-final, Pixel Lumina lost to CGN Esports in the VCL EMEA Last Chance Qualifier 2026. That defeat followed wins over FOKUS and Twisted Saints Esports in the same event.

Aurora’s lineup features Boo, chiwa, Derke, B1SK and trexx. Derke joined straight after Valorant Champions 2026, where his Vitality side lost the grand final 3-1 to LOUD.

Aurora now face the winner of xXxMasterProMegaTeamxXx versus F9 EICAR. That final decides seeding for the Kickoff Qualifier Playoffs. Aurora are already listed as qualified for the playoffs through Qualifier 1, so the final is about position rather than survival.

— Aurora Valorant (@Aurora_Valorant) November 10, 2026

The wider prize is a place at VCT EMEA Kickoff 2027. Europe will supply half of the four non-partner sides heading to the event, Riot Games said, while Türkiye and MENA each send a single team. Kickoff itself will be played offline at the Riot Games Arena in Berlin with 12 teams.

The rest of the European field is still taking shape. Europe Qualifier 2 is scheduled for 12 to 15 November and is also played as single-elimination best-of-three brackets.

#4172. Nioh 3’s generous demo is out now, and your progress carries over to the full game

If you’re looking for a way to check out one of the biggest releases of early 2026, Team Ninja has made it easy for you.

Nioh 3 is one of the most anticipated games of 2026, and it’s easily among the biggest releases of February. We’re a few days away from the start of that month, however, but we don’t have to wait until then to actually play Team Ninja’s next major release.

The previously announced demo has arrived, and it’s one any fan of action games should check out, especially if you missed the PlayStation-exclusive beta held last year.

Unlike previous tests, the Nioh 3 demo is available on PC and PS5, just like the main game. This is pretty new for the series, which has typically launched first on PlayStation before coming to PC months later.

The Nioh 3 demo includes a decent portion of content from the beginning of the game. It’s enough to show off the core duality mechanic, letting you switch between the Samurai and Ninja styles at will. It also includes a preview of the game’s open field level design, which makes it sit somewhere between full open world and the more linear level design of past Nioh games.

Feedback from the previous beta has been implemented into the demo (and full release), so you may see some familiar faces, as well as areas you visited before - assuming you played that one.

Another big reason why you might want to grab the Nioh 3 demo is that your progress in it will carry over to the full version. This includes the character creator, too, meaning you can spend all day perfecting your character without having to worry about missing out on playing the actual game.

The demo even supports online multiplayer for up to three players, in case you come to Nioh for co-op. If you complete the available content, you’ll earn an in-game bonus in the full version. This is something Team Ninja has done with past Nioh titles, of course.

This time, your reward is the Twin-Snake Helmet. Just make sure you complete the demo before February 15.

Nioh 3 is out February 6 on PC, and PlayStation 5.

#4170. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – November 6, 2026

This week and weekend is all about the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, one of the few games I feel deserves the title of masterpiece. And the remake is really well done! I got every heart piece, every Gold Skulltala, the Goron Sword, and the biggest pouch for every one of my items over the course of the review... but I am contemplating jumping right back in for another go.

We also revealed our next cover and in case you missed the announcement it is... pause for effect... Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis! It's an awesome cover that celebrates the history of Lara Croft, and along with a cover story on the game, we also have a big retrospective on the series. I highly recommend subscribing to get your issue if you haven't already.

But it wasn't all just Zelda and Tomb Raider this week. Below you will find a list of weekend play recommendations, but before that... some of our biggest stories of the week.

We have been writing a lot about The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time remake this week because it is one of 2026's most exciting games, and it's real good. The remake is not particularly surprising. It mostly sticks to the trajectory of the original game, but there is a reason it is considered one of the best games of all time. It also looks and plays amazing.

You can read the full review here (or watch the video above), but we also have a big interview with the game's producers (one of whom worked on the original Ocarina of Time, and one who directed Breath of the Wild among many other Zelda games), some details about the Easter Eggs that did and did not make it into the remake, and a very handy tip for the game if you happen to be playing with a Switch 2 Pro controller.

World of Warcraft: Forever is out now and it’s a great time to jump into the revamped and expanded version of a project that changed online games forever back in 2004. A thousand new quests, multiple new zones, countless revamps, and an impressively stunning visual overhaul make it the perfect time to jump in for anyone who’s ever been curious to explore Azeroth.

2022's Escape Academy was a sneaky little puzzle game that surprised me and its sequel released this week. Taking place in a school obsessed with puzzles, you play as a student who must make their way through a series of escape rooms. The puzzles are clever, and the setting is charming, but the secret weapon is the local, split-screen co-op. Solving puzzles together is fun especially when one player needs to look at one section of a room to help dictate a solution on the other side of the room. My wife and I both love video games, but rarely play co-op games together just because of our disparate, individual tastes. But Escape Room is one we enjoyed together and we're so far enjoying the sequel. My only complaint so far is... I wish it ran a little better.

While we collectively use the term here for the sake of familiarity, I’m always a bit hesitant in my own mind to label a game under the wide banner of “Metroidvania.” In part, that’s because I think the two referenced games (Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night) are actually more different than they might appear at first glance. Gloomsoft’s recent release, Moadra, recognizes that distinction, crafting a game that draws heavy inspiration from the specific tradition of Super Metroid, even while presenting an intriguing and atmospheric fiction that is great fun to discover. In movement, actions, and exploration, Moadra feels remarkably similar to  the best of the 2D Metroid games. A scanning tool also leans into the Metroid inspirations, revealing details about the weird alien world you’re navigating. If you’ve been hungry for a game that scratches that particular itch of sci-fi gear/ability-gated exploration, I think you’ll find a lot to love in this game.

I get the Marvel fatigue we've all been experiencing. There are a lot of games and a lot of movies and a lot of TV shows and many are good, but lately most feel like homework. For those reasons, you'd be forgiven for dismissing the 2021 Guardians of the Galaxy game, but I promise you it is good. For one, it is standalone. It does not directly tie to any specific Marvel media. No homework necessary. And for two, it's just a really good game with an affecting story and a unique take on the characters that most of us met for the first time in the movies. And, for the BioWare fans out there mourning the loss of Mass Effect, this game has some Mass Effect energy. It's available on Switch 2 this week and I happily recommend it, especially if you missed it five years ago.

This exclusively two-player board game features a fun mix of activities. You act as both a dungeon architect, and an adventurer delving into said dungeons. Each player creates their own version of a challenging dungeon filled with traps, monsters, and treasures.

But you’re also forced to take on the dangers of your opponent’s crafted dungeon, to see who manages to come out on top. If you have fond memories of the hidden-info nature of old games like Battleship, but you want some greater strategic depth and fantasy flavor thrown in, this one is a great pick.

#4169. Data Shows New Tactical Shooter Port Struck Gold With Console Plans

The surprise announcement of a Squad console port hit harder than a tank rolling through an undefended spawn point.

Taking the world’s most popular tactical shooter and moving to a platform that is typically associated with run-and-gun titles like Call of Duty and Overwatch was a bold move, but the numbers are finally in, and it looks like Offworld Industries played a blinder.

The battles on the Ottoman Front are about to get deadlier as Gallipoli targets hitreg issues.

The Squad console alpha test ran from October 16 to October 25, with a free experience limited exclusively to the PlayStation 5. During the nine days of testing, console players got to try a battle between the Ukrainian Armed Forces and the Chinese People’s Liberation Army.

Although Squad will have full crossplay between PC, PS5, and XBOX Series X/S, the test servers disabled it to give Sony’s faithful a smoother introduction to the game.

Today, OWI has finally published the data from the playtest, and the results are quite encouraging.

According to a social media post by the official Squad account today, just over 110 thousand PS5 players participated in the playtest.

That number in a vacuum doesn’t say much, but what’s impressive is that the Squad playtest led to over 50 thousand wishlists on PlayStation 5 alone, meaning a conversion rate of around 45%. Many an indie dev would caution that treating wishlists as guaranteed sales is a highway to heartbreak, and they’d be right, but at the present moment it’s still a showcase of the positive effect of the playtesting sessions.

The strong reception to the Squad PS5 alpha preview is also reflected in the player ratings. According to OWI, the game closed the testing sessions with a 4.5 out of 5 score. The PC version of Squad has an 83% positive rating on Steam and a 4.3 out of 5 score on the Epic Games Store, landing the console port slightly ahead of its peers, but ultimately in the same bracket.

Squad first came out in 2015, with humble beginnings as a crowdfunded spiritual successor to Battlefield 2’s Project Reality mod. The early versions of the game feel like a far cry from what we call Squad today, especially on the technical side.

According to producer Peter Maurice (full interview here), Squad is done “turning that corner where a lot of the major tech investment is done”, and that has allowed the team at Offworld Industries to turn its focus to new platforms and content.

Taking the world’s most popular tactical shooter and moving to a platform that is typically associated with run-and-gun titles like Call of Duty and Overwatch was a bold move

Currently, Squad runs on Unreal Engine 5.7. The transition from Unreal Engine 4 was “a massive challenge for a small studio,” but the performance benefits were felt on PC once the game found its footing.

According to Maurice, OWI has been planning a console port for as long as 3 years, but the project only transitioned from an idea into reality about a year ago, following the release of space bug shooter Starship Troopers Extermination. The studio was able to move developers who had worked on bringing this game to console and put them to work on Squad, making the transition a lot smoother.

The next big challenge for Squad’s console release will be building a community that can support itself. As Maurice explained to me, consoles do not have a “veterans that have been with us for years like on PC,” and that means players will need the game to help people learn even when a more experienced player is not around.

Squad is coming to PlayStation 5 and XBOX Series X/S sometime in 2027. Secret Mode’s Project Marketing Manager, Matthew Beckett, says a future playtest session is possible, but more info on that later.

#4166. Petit Planet Hands-On Preview – Creature Comforts

Petit Planet marks Hoyoverse’s maiden voyage into the life sim genre popularized by games like Animal Crossing, Stardew Valley, and, most recently, Pokémon Pokopia. The creators of Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, and Zenless Zone Zero have crafted well-received, lucrative free-to-play gacha games across several disparate genres; Petit Planet, fittingly, sees it try to attract yet another world of players. It’s been a year since I first played Petit Planet’s initial alpha test, and I spent a couple of more hours exploring its cozy cosmos at the Hoyoverse Media Tour in Seoul, South Korea. Although what I played has not dramatically changed my opinion of the game – it remains a delightful, if familiar, good time – speaking to its lead designer who goes by the single name Murphy and lead artist Yunli Huang helped shed light on how Petit Planet will differentiate itself from contemporaries and its approach to multiplayer, storytelling, and monetization.

The game’s premise centers on a customizable protagonist who sets out to populate their own personal planet (which is about the size of King Kai’s world from Dragon Ball Z). Although you are ostensibly human, everyone else is a talking animal. Your mentor of sorts is a chillax sheepdog named Mobai, who enjoys wearing straw hats and dropping his catchphrase/life mantra “Mo worries” and “Mo Rush.” The business-minded Glenn the Squirrel is a shopkeeper and seems like a cuter, less aggressive Tom Nook. Yunghou is a shy fox who enjoys farming and has the slightest hint of a southern accent. These critters and many more inhabit your planet, which you’ll grow from an empty (but vibrant) rock into a bustling village filled with homes, businesses, crops, decor, and, of course, neighbors.

Story is rarely a hook for a genre that largely promotes creating your own fun through the emergent moments with your neighbors and friends in multiplayer. Still, after Pokémon Pokopia presented an unexpectedly wild and fascinating tale, I ask if players should bother getting invested in a grander narrative à la Genshin Impact. The short answer seems to be “not so much.”

“Unlike other Hoyoverse games, there is no such main plot,” Murphy explains in my group interview. “There will be a main story at the beginning, but the main purpose is just to guide the players, get more familiar with the setting and the world. But the whole narrative of this game will be more fragmented. For example, if you look at those descriptions of those items, there will be a lot of content and narrative behind it. If you look at the description of creatures, many of them are real creatures in real world, and you get to learn more knowledge of this creature by reading those descriptions. And also, we've developed a very comprehensive narrative for each of our neighbors, so that is also part of our, called like, main plot, main narrative, because we want to make this world more like more lively and a more livable world. So that is how we treat narrative in this game."

While players who enjoy a substantial story to propel them through a game may be disappointed, those looking to unwind with a laid-back experience should be pleased. Hoyoverse is designing Petit Planet to be a no-pressure experience to enjoy at your leisure, hence why it emphasizes it as a life sim more than a management sim. There are no complicated stats to manage; simple inputs make it easy to pick up and play; imperfection is encouraged, with Hoyoverse comparing the experience to doodling as a child: your creation may not be perfect, but you had fun bringing your imagination to life.

I spent the first hour of my roughly two-and-a-half-hour session starting from scratch to see if any notable changes were made to this introductory portion in the last year. If there are any differences, they’re imperceptible because I wen went through the same onboarding of learning how to catch bugs and fish, building your first home, inviting your first neighbor, and farming crops, all while growing a magical sapling that, after performing enough tasks, blooms into a full tree that brings new life and mechanics to your world as it grows. Performing special tasks for residents, from completing requests to simply interacting with them, grows their bond, which, when high enough, will entice them to move in. For veteran genre fans, it’s a familiar song and dance. What I did notice this time around is how refreshingly quick the onboarding is. You have all of these foundational mechanics within the first 45 to 50 minutes, which is a nice pace. It was a good refresher for some foundational mechanics I’d forgotten since I last played, but it created an appetite to dive deeper.

Thankfully, Hoyoverse provided a second build set many hours into the game to give an idea of how planets can evolve. This build was set during winter, one of Petit Planet’s revolving seasons that alter the environment and introduce themed cosmetics and decor for players and residents. Sporting winter gear, I ran around the snow-covered planet, which was densely populated with shops, homes, and neighbors. I was initially greeted by unfamiliar faces named Trixie and Kookoo, who provided weather forecasts and news reports reminiscent of Isabelle from Animal Crossing and Callie and Marie from Splatoon. My sparse quest log was tricky to tackle since they revolved around mechanics I had no context for, such as setting up Vignettes. These are essentially templates for unique scenes filled out by dropping the correct furniture pieces in their layout; in this case, I had to set up an outdoor movie on the beach.

I only spent roughly an hour with this late build, and my biggest takeaway was simply how dense and lovely the village looked. A lot of work went into crafting this build, which boasted a farm filled with different crops (with unlockable recipes to create dishes from them), crafting tables to build furniture from collectible blueprints, and several shops, including Glenn’s to purchase a revolving selection of decor items. None of what I saw surprised me, however. Petit Planet so far checks many of the boxes you’d expect and want from a life sim. My cursory tour of a later-game planet did little to reveal any big new ideas, but what I did experience seemed perfectly cromulent.

My biggest question regards multiplayer. As much as I enjoy Animal Crossing: New Horizons and Pokémon Pokopia as solo experiences, playing with friends feels like a mean joke because of the tedious number of hoops to jump through just to invite other players into your world. And even once your buddy arrives, interactions are disappointingly limited. When I ask if Petit Planet offers a comparatively frictionless multiplayer experience, Murphy vaguely assures smoother sailing. “The multiplayer experience is a very important part of our game because, just as the interaction with NPCs, the interaction with other players is also a form of building up emotional connection to this game, and we want to provide that kind of experience to our players.” More specifically, Murphy cites features such as dynamic server load adjustments based on player counts and the option to allow or ban visiting players from taking resources from your planet to prevent griefing.

As a free-to-play Hoyoverse game, monetization is a major talking point. In Petit Planet’s case, the team agrees that rolling for neighbors gacha-style would be strange and defeats the spirit of the genre. Instead, all monetization will revolve around cosmetics; players can unlock new furniture and themed decor sets, outfits, and other cosmetic accessories for their character. Unlocking a full themed set of decor earns currency points, and there are myriad reward meters to fill for performing mundane tasks like greeting residents or catching bugs. It remains to be seen if and how Petit Planet’s progression begins nudging players into opening their wallets, but Hoyoverse promises it will be an experience that deemphasizes grinding.

I also briefly checked out the recently announced Switch 2 version of Petit Planet. My impressions after about 15 minutes of playtime: it’s fine. It sometimes ran noticeably hitchier than the PC version I spent most of my time with, but it seems perfectly adequate so far and, hopefully, will be a smooth experience when it launches sometime next year.

Since life sims require more than a couple of hours to fully reveal their quality, it was tough to get a read on Petit Planet even with this new showing. The game looks beautiful thanks to Hoyoverse’s signature sharp and colorful visual style. It has a relaxing vibe, and feels mechanically decent for the most part. In short, it seems broadly fine and like a respectable take on the genre. I suspect its biggest appeal will be that it will receive what Animal Crossing: New Horizons lacked: years of constant, substantial support.

Hoyoverse is very good about keeping fans of its games well fed with regular updates for years on end, and I don’t expect it to stop now. The idea of a seemingly well-made spin on Animal Crossing that’s free to download and, unless it completely bombs, will almost certainly receive years of new content is enticing on paper. I imagine this is the reason Petit Planet is coming to Switch 2 next year, where it can lure in Animal Crossing and Pokopia players before other consoles. PC and mobile players, meanwhile, must only wait until December 4 when Petit Planet fully launches to see if it has the chops to stand alongside the coziest giants of the genre.

Here are the start and end times for the second Spellcasters Chronicles closed beta, as well as what's new in this latest test.

Quantic Dream has opened up its upcoming fantasy MOBA for a second closed beta weekend starting from today, January 29, until 9AM UTC on Monday February 2.

The closed beta is for PC only in Europe, Asia and North America and potential players can register to join the waitlist for a key at the game’s official website or on the Spellcasters Chronicles Steam page. Players who had access to the first closed beta will automatically have access to the second, but you can sign up on both the site and Steam to increase your chances of entry.

The MOBA genre is competitive in every sense and Quantic Dream is trying to break into it with a Magic the Gathering-esque spin on the format. Players build a deck of cards before queuing into teams of 3, then face off as battling mages, summoning creatures, building fortifications and casting spells rather than choosing a Hero with unique abilities in the traditional MOBA style.

Beta content includes a new map, 6 new spells and 5 new summon creatures for your deck, as well as 3 new buildings too.

Also new for this second closed beta is an introduction and tutorial for some of the game’s finer details, as well as a text chat for strategising and much-needed player reporting system to go with it. It will also feature early versions of the Spellcaster customisation system and ranked matches.

#4164. Reinstated Aurora Gaming beat F9 EICAR to win Valorant Europe Qualifier 1

Aurora Gaming came from a map down to beat F9 EICAR 2-1 and win the first VCT EMEA Kickoff Europe open qualifier. The win came days after they were put back into the bracket when the UK team BONK was disqualified for cheating.

The VCT EMEA Kickoff: Europe Qualifier 2027 decider got under way at 18:45. The series began on Lotus. Aurora’s chiwa was named most valuable player of the series.

The Aurora roster lists Boo, chiwa, Derke, B1SK and trexx. F9 EICAR, based in France, fielded Kipperman, Destrian, Tenshi, izana and Geekkooo.

Aurora’s run nearly ended early. BONK, a UK Valorant roster, beat them 2-1 in the round of 32 on 6 November. That result followed a comeback from 3-11 down on Bind. Riot’s ruling against BONK reversed Aurora’s exit. Every BONK player and registered team member was provisionally suspended. Project 100K and ycatble returned to the bracket along with Aurora.

The qualifier left no room for error. It was a single-elimination bracket for 256 teams, and every match was a best-of-three. Once reinstated, Aurora did not drop a map before the final. They beat Pixel Lumina 2-0 in the second semi-final.

In the first semi-final, xXxMasterProMegaTeamxXx fell 2-1 to F9 EICAR. The French side had arrived at the qualifier in mixed form. F9 EICAR lost 0-2 to WIP Esports in VCL France: Revolution Stage 2 2026 and were twice beaten 1-2 by Mandatory. A 2-1 result against Esprit Shōnen was their only victory in that run.

The Elo power rankings show the gap on paper. F9 EICAR sit at rank 241, with a rating of 1405 and a 6-16 record in 22 rated matches. Aurora are unranked.

The final still carried weight. Seeding for the playoff stage would be decided by the result, Insider Gaming reported.

The stakes are clear. Under Riot’s 2027 system, four non-partner teams will reach VCT EMEA Kickoff. Two will come from Europe, one from Türkiye and one from the Middle East and North Africa.

— Aurora Valorant (@Aurora_Valorant) November 10, 2026

That leaves European hopefuls chasing places at a 12-team LAN event. VCT 2027 EMEA Kickoff will be run by Riot Games at the Riot Games Arena in Berlin.

The playoff field is not yet complete. The top four teams from each open qualifier move on, and the second Europe open qualifier is set for 12 to 15 November. The playoffs will use a modified double-elimination bracket of best-of-three matches, with a best-of-five grand final. The top two finishers earn places at VCT 2027 EMEA Kickoff, whose window runs from 14 January to 7 February.
