#4096. Riot Reveals Full League of Legends Conversion, But You’ll Have to Wait

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

All the time, live service titles are forced to pump out content to avoid stagnating over time, anything to catch the attention of new players and reignite the passion of old returning faces. Sometimes, games feel the need to really shake things up, especially if they’re on the older side of release dates. Today, it seems, League of Legends is joining this number.

Stats for Star Wars Zero Company are out, and the results are showing some major Clone supremacy.

Announced at the tail end of Worlds 2026, Riot has showcased what it calls “League of Legends: New Dawn”, a total revamp of League’s client, mechanics, and visuals to bring it up to snuff with the modern age.

All these changes and more have been requested by the community for years, but now that they’re right around the corner, a vocal segment seems incredibly unimpressed.

League of Legends is a title that has slowly but surely been pulled down by the weight of its ancient code, forcing the dev team at Riot to totally rewrite decent chunks of the client inside and out to make new proper content. This hiccup has been the excuse for missing features and slow updates for ages, and it looks like Riot is finally ready to put their foot down.

With a new proper rival in the MOBA space via Valve’s Deadlock, Riot has had a bit of a fire lit under them, pushing them to speed up development in this massive overhaul. New runes, new lobby animations, and a fully reworked map are just some of the new content coming in this proper total overhaul of the game, looking to lead League into a New Dawn for the coming years.

It seems like every member of the classic League roster is also getting a full visual overhaul, bringing them up to the quality showcased by recent releases like Locke and Zaahen. Compounded with the rumors of a sequel series to Arcane in the works, it seems like Riot is focusing hard on celebrating and bringing focus back to base League of Legends, rather than highlighting the universe with different titles.

Sometimes, games feel the need to really shake things up, especially if they’re on the older side of release dates

Riot stayed vague on a lot of the actual reworked mechanics, but with 2 minutes of footage out and a promise of more coming in January, current players and fans who have fallen off the wagon both have a reason to keep an eye out. They say League comes for every PC gamer eventually, and a few good changes could make its tendrils all the harder to avoid.

A sizable amount of the community response to the announcement has actually been rather negative, tossing shade towards the game for looking too “mobile game-y” after its vibrant new coat of paint. This marks a phenomenon I’ve seen throughout longtime free-to-play titles: a confusing mix of wanting developer attention without actually wanting much changed.

The Counter-Strike community is another proponent of this practice, clearly wanting Valve’s attention through skins and patches, without actually wanting any real part of the CS tempo changed. Now, for longtime fans, this can be understandable; after all, nobody wants their favorite game suddenly changed into something totally different. However, every live service title, no matter the age, needs new blood.

The aging visuals and code of League have clearly been the largest stopgap to its constant evolution, and the promises set forth by Riot for League of Legends: New Dawn are seriously hopeful, opening the door for new players and those who have grown tired of the shakiest part of the MOBA giant. Years of work and slow improvement are clear through every inch of the visuals, I just need to see how it plays!

#4095. Marathon may actually have a shot as Server Slam hits it big on Steam

Marathon's latest public open weekend has kicked off, and it looks like enough people have showed up to play it.

Things are officially looking better for Marathon. The game’s Server Slam, essentially an open beta that’s freely available everywhere, has kicked off. This is the last chance for anyone curious about Bungie’s next big game to play it before it officially goes on sale next week.

Considering how unpopular the game has been throughout its development, and judging by the feedback from earlier closed beta tests, the turnout for the Server Slam is definitely encouraging.

The Marathon Server Slam has been online for a little over 12 hours on Steam, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. Only one of those platforms shares player numbers, of course, but it's enough to offer some visibility into how popular the test has been.

Immediately after servers went live, Marathon shot up the Steam most played charts. The game quickly achieved a peak of 143,621 concurrent players (via SteamDB), which is very respectable. Given that the Server Slam will be available for the entire weekend, there’s every chance the numbers will go up.

These figures are particularly encouraging when you look at Arc Raiders, the current top dog in the extraction shooter space, and the game that stole Marathon’s thunder last year when the two of them were being promoted by their publishers. Marathon, of course, got delayed out of 2025, which allowed Arc Raiders to launch first. It, of course, ended up proving that extraction shooters can be mainstream hits.

Like Marathon, Arc Raiders hosted its own server slam just a few days before its launch. That open test attracted 189,668 concurrent players at its peak, which is not that far off from Marathon’s so far.

Assuming positive word of mouth continues, more players are bound to jump in over the weekend and perhaps get Marathon to match or even exceed Arc Raiders’ record. At any rate, this is good news for beleaguered Bungie and points to what could be a big launch.

Marathon arrives March 5 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.

#4093. The Sims 4 is getting paid mods, and a new in-game currency to pay for them

The Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis announced The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two new destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

The two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

Created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature launches, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a new virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

In order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

In the blog post announcing the new features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.

#4091. God Of War Sons Of Sparta Gets PS4 Version And New Content Next Monday

It's been about nine months since Sony Santa Monica and Mega Cat Studios dropped God of War Sons of Sparta as a surprise reveal and launch during a State of Play. If you haven't checked it out yet, the developers are giving you some new reasons to today, unveiling two new modes and a new platform: PlayStation 4.

If you don't remember, God of War Sons of Sparta is a prequel spin-off of the God of War series, showing protagonist Kratos as a 13-year-old soldier, long before his god-killing days. The game features 2D combat and a Metroidvania-style map, along with a fully voiced cast of characters including Scott Menville (who you might recognize as Robin in Teen Titans) as Kratos' brother Deimos, Jack Quaid (who will voice a different character in God of War Laufey next year), and TC Carson, who returns from the original trilogy as the voice of adult Kratos.

Announced in a post on the PlayStation Blog today, Sons of Sparta is making the jump back to Sony's previous console, which is now (brace yourself) 13 years old. Sons of Sparta's 2D pixel art is far less demanding than the other God of War entries, though, so it's no surprise this was possible – it's mainly surprising that they're doing it at all.

For PS5 players who already own the game, developer Mega Cat is also adding two new modes: Hermes Mode and Erebus Mode. Hermes Mode, named after the Greek god of wind, mail, and speed, is a speedrun mode that encourages you to beat the game as quickly as possible, complete with a split-based timer in the upper right-hand corner of the screen. Meanwhile, Erebus Mode, named after one of the domains of the underworld (you'll be familiar with it if you've played the Hades games), makes the game far deadlier as Kratos and all his foes die in a single hit. You'll have to wait until you beat the game once to unlock Erebus Mode, but you can access Hermes Mode from a fresh save by entering the following (and semi-familiar) code in the start menu: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, L1, R1, Touchpad.

The free update and PS4 version will be available next Monday, November 16, at midnight local time. For more Sons of Sparta, check out our review. For more God of War, bad news: God of War Laufey was just delayed until May.

#4090. 10 JRPGs Launching in 2027 You Should Keep on Your Radar

Murillo Zerbinatto is a JRPG enthusiast, writer, and editor. He has played over 300 RPGs during his gaming career, with 90% of them being JRPGs.

The pandemic sure threw a wrench into many developers' plans, which was understandable. However, as soon as the situation began to normalize, many games that were delayed or suffered internal setbacks started getting revealed with official release dates. It feels like ever since 2023 we have been living through a run of great releases, with banger after banger.

Furthermore, JRPG fans have been well served since then. A new title keeps coming out, whether from indie developers, veterans who left their former companies to start their own studios, or fresh remasters and remakes popping up. I, for one, would love some peace and downtime to just play casually, and I thought 2027 would bring that relief, but I was mistaken. The year hasn't even begun, and my backlog is already clogging up again. Let us take a look at a few upcoming JRPGs in 2027 that you should definitely keep on your radar.

Which 2026 JRPGs are the best according to their Metascore?

Terranigma brings back a classic from the SNES, a JRPG that formed part of the legendary Quintet Trilogy. It functions more as a direct port than a full remaster, but it remains extremely welcome nonetheless. Terranigma never originally launched in North America, only in Japan and Europe, meaning many players from back in the day never had the chance to experience this action RPG.

In Terranigma, we play as Ark on a mission to restore Earth. And by Earth, I mean our actual planet, as all the continents are based on real-world geography that we gradually bring back to life. To do this, Ark uses a real-time combat system driven by level-ups and spells you buy along the way. The most enjoyable aspect of Terranigma is witnessing the world-building sidequests unfold as you visit villages and restore them. It is a fantastic treat for anyone looking to revisit or experience a past JRPG gem through an official release.

Against all odds and to my utmost surprise, SaGa is becoming one of the longest-running and most sprawling series in the Square Enix catalog. I know it is unorthodox and not everyone enjoys its unconventional design, but I love seeing Square keeping the franchise alive, especially through its remakes. Following Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven, Square Enix is delivering a full remake of the third entry titled Romancing SaGa 3: Destinies United.

The remake will include similar enhancements to Revenge of the Seven, such as a revamped turn-based system that heavily emphasizes targeting enemy elemental weaknesses, while retaining core SaGa staples like Glimmer mechanics and open-ended progression where players shape the narrative path. I don't know if it will be as brutally difficult as the original Romancing SaGa 3, which was notorious for softlocking players with its complex progression systems. Still, it will certainly be a feast for fans of the series.

Continuing with upcoming remakes, Atlus is bringing another project to the table: Persona 4 Revival. As the name implies, this is a ground-up remake of the fourth Persona entry, fully modernized with current-gen graphics, overhauled combat mechanics, a re-orchestrated soundtrack, new social activities, extra story events, and expanded dungeon crawling elements inside the TV World.

The best part is being able to revisit what many consider the best Persona game (a statement that could honestly apply to almost any entry in the franchise). Returning to the town of Inaba, we play as the canonically named student Yu Narukami. While keeping up with his daily routine of school life, part-time jobs, and social simulation, he will also need to unravel the mysteries of the TV World alongside fan-favorite Teddie.

Atelier is one of the longest-running JRPG series, with a fanbase more dedicated than a football club. While the overall narrative remains anthological across the franchise, Atelier is organized into distinct subseries. Following the Secret subseries featuring Atelier Ryza, we have the Memories subseries, which kicked off with Atelier Yumia and now continues with Atelier Karia: The Night Kingdom & the Guide of Memories.

Atelier Karia continues the adventure in Aladiss, this time venturing into the underground world of Noctrem. This entry puts players in control of Karia, an amnesiac alchemist. Combat builds upon the real-time foundation established in Yumia, with Karia introducing a strategic layer that lets players pause combat to execute command skills or parry incoming enemy attacks. I won't say playing Atelier Yumia beforehand is strictly mandatory, but if you want full context, it might be the ideal route.

It's no exaggeration to say that Eternal Anima is one of my most anticipated JRPGs of 2027. The game was unveiled during a Nintendo Direct, and while I initially fell in love with its charming pixel art, it first looked like just another solid indie release. That changed once I looked into the talent behind the project, including industry veterans like Kazushige Nojima, a legendary Final Fantasy writer, and director Katsuhisa Higuchi, who worked as a battle programmer on several Final Fantasy titles and directed Monster Hunter Stories 2.

Early previews for Eternal Anima are singing high praise, spotlighting its refreshing turn-based combat, its time-travel mechanics (a narrative trope I never get tired of), and how seamlessly both elements interlock. The story follows Wade alongside an eclectic party gathered from different timelines. Combat features a mechanic called Future Sight that previews enemy moves, showing who they plan to target and the exact damage output, which elevates tactical planning and should be a joy to experiment with. I will be sitting in the front row waiting for Eternal Anima.

If you loved Final Fantasy Resonance, then it's time for more JRPG love, Jobs, and pixel art.

Final Fantasy VII Revelation needs no introduction and stands as one of the world's most anticipated JRPGs of 2027. We can wait for The Game Awards to hand out the Most Anticipated Game trophy, and if Final Fantasy VII Revelation doesn't take it home, feel free to call me out in the comments. Serving as the conclusion to the Final Fantasy VII remake trilogy, it appears to have refined everything that made its predecessors spectacular, pushing combat, exploration, and player freedom to new heights.

Narratively, it will conclude the main arc, though whether it introduces major plot twists remains to be seen. We do know the Weapons are present and look more imposing than ever. Combat introduces two new playable party members, Vincent and Cid, along with the new FITs system, which acts like a Job framework to give each character a broader tactical arsenal. As for traversal, with the Highwind at our disposal, Square Enix stated that world exploration is completely open, leaving route decisions entirely up to the player. Certain regions will have higher level thresholds, nudging players to tackle them later, but the overall scope looks immensely promising. Final Fantasy VII Revelation, the year is yours.

We now shift to games targeted for 2027 that lack specific day-and-date release slots, which leaves them open to potential schedule shifts. That said, if one developer rarely delays its titles, it is Nintendo. Because of that track record, when Nintendo announced Xenoblade Genesis for 2027, I knew with confidence I would be playing it next year.

Xenoblade Genesis marks the latest chapter in the Xenoblade saga. Whether it functions as a direct narrative sequel to the Chronicles arc remains unconfirmed, but it continues under the direction of Monolith Soft and series creator Tetsuya Takahashi. The reveal trailer omitted gameplay, focusing instead on narrative cutscenes that showcased story beats and main characters. The artistic direction initially drew mixed reactions from some fans for leaning closer to Fire Emblem than traditional Xenoblade, but I personally loved every bit of it, including the medieval aesthetic.

Knowing Monolith Soft, Xenoblade Genesis will feature a colossal world, an overhauled battle system, unorthodox progression mechanics, and endless features that will sink hundreds of hours into this new universe. Did I mention Yoko Shimomura is composing the soundtrack? That alone means it's a fantastic time to update my Spotify playlists.

In this new JRPG, players take control of Asch and Finé as they set out to prevent a world-ending catastrophe known as the Lightfall. Rev. NOiR. is an action RPG, but it features a tactical time-stop mechanic similar to Final Fantasy VII Remake, letting you pause combat to issue skill commands through a visually stylish menu. Deep gameplay details remain sparse for now, but as mentioned, I'm choosing to trust the project and will be ready on day one once Rev.Noir. locks in its official release date.

Here is another franchise that requires zero introduction. Pokémon Winds & Waves is being touted as the first truly high-fidelity graphical Pokémon title, which would certainly be a milestone achievement for Game Freak. Given its oceanic setting packed with islands and open seas, it has every tool required to expand the open-world framework of Pokémon Scarlet and Violet to unprecedented heights, complete with fresh traversal mechanics.

No specifics have been revealed regarding the battle mechanics. However, it will likely preserve the turn-based structure of its mainline predecessor while leaving real-time action gameplay to the Legends spinoff series. For anyone jumping into Pokémon Winds & Waves, three traditional elemental starter companions await: the puppy Pombon, the gecko Gecqua, and the bean chick Browt. I will almost certainly end up picking Gecqua.

I want to start by noting that, according to the developers and director Tetsuya Nomura himself, Kingdom Hearts IV will definitely launch in 2027 and won't face delays. Square Enix confirmed that internal development is progressing smoothly, setting up the long-awaited return of Sora's adventure in Quadratum, complete with new characters (along with returning faces for those who played the mobile entries) and a fresh selection of Disney worlds.

In terms of core design and gameplay structure, we can expect a polished take on the series' classic loop: Sora travels from world to world, adapts to local rules, meets regional protagonists, and aids them in their struggles. It is a charming formula, and I would not have it any other way. Officially, only the world of Coco has been formally revealed, though a leak stemming from Steam achievements unveiled several others. I won't share those details here to keep you safe from spoilers, but if you want to look them up, do so at your own risk.

From Eternal Sonata to Triangle Strategy, revisit seven underrated JRPGs that launched near major blockbusters and struggled for attention.

Diablo 4’s next, long-awaited Developer Update finally airs today. This meaty livestream was first announced nearly a month ago, when Blizzard initially revealed that the game’s next class is the Warlock.

The Warlock is one of two classes coming to Diablo 4 with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion. The first, the Paladin, is already available in the game for anyone who pre-orders the expansion. The Warlock will instead arrive alongside the expansion on April 28.

The Developer Update will also include a first look at the game’s next season (Season 12), currently set for March 10. This mini season will only last until the expansion’s release, so it’s going to be interesting to see what it brings to the game.

You’ll be able to watch the showcase live at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT on Diablo 4’s official YouTube, Twitch, and Twitter channels. We’ve embedded the YouTube and Twitch players below for your convenience.

Among the topics the Developer Update will cover are the Killstreaks system, as well as Bloodstained items. As always, you can also expect a Q&A segment at the end of the show, and I imagine there’s going to be a few about the Warlock.

Just don't expect to hear about it too soon. Here's the confirmation:

id Software: "We're incredibly excited about our next project, a new game from our teams in Texas and Frankfurt, with game direction once again by Hugo Martin. It'll be some time before we're ready to share more but we can't wait for you to see what we're working on."

"I reported in July that id were in the “early stages of a new Doom game” and now it’s confirmed."

This follows the news earlier this year of layoffs at id Software, which led to a statement from the studio, noting how the team was now "about the same size" as it was when making DOOM (2016).

id Software has previously released DOOM (2016) and DOOM Eternal on the Switch with the help of Panic Button. There's no mention about it bringing across the latest title, DOOM: The Dark Ages, to Nintendo's new hybrid platform.

#4086. Ocarina Of Time Zelda Notes Officially Reveal Number One Cause Of Death

In 1998, if you wanted to know how everyone else was faring in Ocarina of Time, you'd have to ask your friends in the playground between rumors of a hidden Sky Temple. Or maybe you'd scour some old-school message boards like N64.com and AOL, long before the days of Reddit and centralized social media.

It's a little different for today's kids. Now, there's a dedicated Zelda Notes section on the Nintendo Switch app that keeps track of all the stats, so you only need to swipe on your smartphone to find out who is dying to what. It's got a little less of that tactile hubbub of the playground rumor mill, but there are some interesting details to come out of it.

As reported by GoNintendo, the Zelda Notes not only provide personalized playtime data, but global data. If you die to an enemy, you get lumped into a statistic that everyone can gawk at. Funnily enough, not much has changed since the day of ASCII-art GamesFaq guides, when authors would urge that you "run through the green muck" because it "hurts less than if you go near a ReDead." Even now, in the remake, they're the leading cause of death in Hyrule.

It'd be interesting if there were statistics from the '90s that we could compare this to. I'd imagine that ReDeads and Gibdos would still be the #1 cause of death — though it'd be fascinating to know if people died as little as they have in the remake. Was the original game really harder, or were we just kids who didn't know any better?

We finally got a chance to play The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake and it's still one of the best games ever made.

We don't have an app that handily compiles stats like this from 1998, but there are some old internet forums that do shed light on what Ocarina of Time players thought at the time. On the Ushi No Tane forum, one player wrote that they "hate" ReDeads specifically because "they hump your face." Others in the comments said it was "the scream" that did it, or simply that they "freak me out."

In 2006, someone posted to the Neoseeker forums asking, "What's your most annoying enemy?" The comments called out the Tektites, Wallmasters, and yes, the ReDeads. And in 2003, IGN described Dark Link as "the most annoying mini-boss in the history of Zelda," so if you're dying to him in the remake, just know that a stressed-out guide writer was suffering through the same fight you were over 20 years ago.

The big Diablo 4 Developer Update has indeed delivered the goods. One of the livestream’s big topics was, of course, the game’s upcoming mini-season, which is set to kick off next week and run until the launch of Lord of Hatred, the game’s anticipated next expansion.

You can tell Blizzard wanted to have a bit of fun with Season of Slaughter, as many of its major features make it look like a limited-time event, but there is plenty to be excited about here.

Season of Slaughter kicks off March 11, and will run until the following season kicks off April 28, with the launch of the Lord of Hatred expansion. Many of the season’s biggest additions were available to preview in the 2.6.0 Public Test Realm.

Patch 2.6.0, as you might have guessed, is the one that will kick off the slaughter next week. The headline feature here is ability to become The Butcher, the iconic in-game boss who randomly invades players’ games.

When you play as The Butcher, you’ll be rewarded the more kills you get in quick succession. Your skills hotbar will transform to become something more fitting of The Butcher, making them more brutal. You’ll also earn a seasonal currency as you play.

Starting the seasonal questline is how you can begin to assume The Butcher’s form. A Taste of Power can be initiated from Gea Kul. Transforming into The Butcher can be done in a few ways. As you play, you’ll earn Meaty Offerings, which can later be spent on Shrines of Slaughter in the new Helltide. Once activated, the shrine will draw more enemies towards you.

If you never venture into PvP zones in Diablo 4, this season may change your mind. The standard PvP combat that could only be found in Fields of Hatred has been replaced with a Ceremony of Slaughter, a new event that rewards you for killing enemies quickly. See it through and The Butcher’s Idol will spawn, allowing you to transform into it.

Elsewhere in the world, you’ll also be able to attain the same power at Slaughterhouses, a new activity type available this season. Inside, you immediately become The Butcher for the entirety of the run.

The Butcher’s arrival also ties into two of the other Season of Slaughter’s more interesting additions. First, the Killstreak system finally arrives in Diablo 4, rewarding you for being as efficient as possible in carving your way through enemies.

Anyone who played Diablo 3 should be familiar with how it works. It kicks off the moment you get a kill, and has a visible timer where you’ll need continue performing the same action to up your streak. The more kills you get, the more often your timer will refresh.

There are five tiers to climb through: Killstreak, Carnage, Devastation, Bloodbath, and Massacre. You’re awarded for the tier you manage to reach before the timer runs out. You’ll earn XP and seasonal rep each time a Killstreak is achieved.

The other Butcher-themed addition is Bloodied Items, which is a new item quality available throughout this season. They play into the Killstreak system to grant you even more power. Bloodied Items come with unique affixes that scale off your Killstreak tier. You’ll see many familiar items in that pool, as any item in the game has a chance to drop as Bloodied. Bloodied Items can also be acquired by earning Fresh Meat.

Even if none of that sounds exciting, you’re probably going to redownload the game for The Paladin free trial, which kicks off alongside the new season on March 11. The trial is only available until March 18, and it lets you try out the Paladin class.

The trial is available across PC, PlayStation, and Xbox. You’ll be able to take the new class for a spin, but your progress will be capped at level 25. The Paladin can be permanently unlocked by buying the Lord of Hatred expansion, as it’s one of two classes the expansion is introducing.

The good news is that any progress you make in the free trial will carry over to the full game if/when you buy the expansion.

Season of Slaughter also kicks off a Doom: The Dark Ages collaboration event. As we’ve come to expect, there’s a very limited free component to the collaboration, in the form of the Doom Reliquary. This is essentially a mini-battle pass that includes the Shield Saw skin, Slayer’s Flair, the head of the Cyberdemon as a back trophy and various other smaller bits.

The more impressive items - such as character skins, will instead be available to purchase for real money. The list includes the Doom Slayer armor, Mecha Dragon Serrat skin for your cat mount, and a Cacodemon pet.

Though the armor skin is cross-class compatible, judging by how much previous collaboration items have cost in Diablo 4, most of us probably won’t be spending that kind of money to get it.

#4084. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – November 13, 2026

Today is Friday the 13th, but let's not dwell on that. Here are some weekend video games to play. Well, actually, here are some of our biggest stories of the week, and then you can check out some weekend game recommendations.

Also, go ahead and make some space on your Xbox or PlayStation hard drive to make room for GTAVI. It's going to be about 200 GB and you can pre-load it now. Delete those games you're not going to return to. Delete all those video clips you'll never watch from every time you get a Trophy on your PlayStation. And you know what? Go ahead and delete Fortnite, too. It's time.

Calling all sickos of The Rootrees Are Dead, Return of the Obra Dinn, The Incident At Galley House, and everything in between: there’s another good deduction game to obsess over. Funeral for the Sun stars a historian who visits an abandoned Latin American town to piece together its turbulent history, chiefly the truth behind the mysterious disappearance of its hundreds of residents (who were, officially speaking, lost in a fire). Supernatural forces allow players to peer into the town’s past to learn about key people potentially responsible for the calamity, who they must identify by name, establish relationships between, and even match younger and older versions of themselves. You even keep track of information using a multi-function notebook à la The Roottrees Are Dead. Boasting an enticing story, a beautiful painterly art direction, and a tight runtime at roughly 8-hours (or less if you’re really on a roll), Funeral for the Sun is a mystery worth unraveling if you need a new deduction game to cozy up with.

NetEase has continued to impress with the pace and quality of its regular updates to Marvel Rivals, which continues today with the release of an 11th season for the superhero battler. Right here at launch, the notable addition is he arrival of X-Men hero Nightcrawler, who BAMFs his way into battle as a strategist, equally capable of healing allies and taking out foes with his sword and brimstone bombs. As is almost always the case right at a new hero’s launch, it can be hard to snag him on the roster on opening day to see how he plays, but once you do, I expect you’ll find him a versatile healer who can pretty dramatically shake up the battlefield, especially with his Ultimate, which basically consolidates allies and enemies together in one central clump for a frenzied exchange of blows. Alongside the new batch of seasonal cosmetics and events to dive into, it’s once again a good time to don your hero outfit and take on some matches.

Pikmin 4 released on Switch 2 this week (or upgraded to Switch 2 depending on how you look at it), and that's a good thing. Pikmin 4 is the best game in the series and the Switch 2 version is the best version. That's great for those who never finished the game (your save does transfer) or skipped Pikmin 4 when it released in 2023, but if you're looking for an excuse to return to the game and play new content, the Dandori Academy addition is underwhelming. You can read my full thoughts here.

Metaphor: ReFantazio, originally released in 2024, is a great RPG from the creators of Persona. And the Persona lineage is obvious throughout the full game. You have to pick and choose where and with whom you should be spending your time, all while a big world-saving RPG with a memorable party of characters plays out in the foreground.

It released this week for Switch 2 and it’s a game that I think would play well on a handheld device. It’s also just a good RPG to play if you missed it previously.

Fun fact: Metaphor: ReFantazio was the game we had lined up to be the next cover when we were temporarily shut down in in 2024. We went to the studio and had a cover drawn up and everything. You can read the full details of the cover story that never was right here.

You can also read Game Informer's review of Metaphor: ReFantazio by following the link.

As we enjoy the final week in a pre-GTA VI world, what better way to gird your loins for next week’s release, so to speak, than by revisiting the last adventures set in Rockstar’s take on Miami? 2002’s Grand Theft Auto: Vice City is a certified classic that, if you’ve never played it, offers nice foundational insight into what Vice City was like in the ’80s (spoiler: it was a lot like Scarface and Miami Vice). Best of all, Vice City is easily available on current platforms with modernized improvements to boot.

If you want to go even further back, chronologically speaking, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories is a prequel set two years before the events of Vice City. Maybe, in some extremely minute way, Vice City Stories lays narrative groundwork for GTA VI. It’s unlikely, but you never know. Originally released for PSP in 2006, Vice City Stories is trickier to play if you don’t own Sony's retired handheld or a PlayStation 2, which it was ported to in 2007. But if you can find the means, there’s no better time to check out this often overlooked chapter of Vice City’s history.

I usually hold off on early access games, to preserve my experience for the finished product, but I just couldn’t resist Slay the Spire 2. The co-op gameplay is an awesome, major change, but even just adding a couple of new characters and cards would have satisfied my cravings. To that end, this week’s free update adds a brand new character, the Fool, who I’m eager to test out.

FYI, this new character is only available on the game’s beta, so you’ll have to go into the game settings on steam, click Properties, then Game Versions & Betas, and then opt into the “public-beta” version of the game to check the new content out. The patch notes for this update specifically say, “We expect to make a great number of content and balance changes before the Fool is ready for the main branch,” so expect frequent tweaks and a bit of a wait before the Fool joins the main Early Access branch. The new beta update also adds two more game modes: Dread and Blitz, which drastically alter your runs. If you want to wait a little while, the team at Mega Crit will refine these options into a more final form. But if you’re like me, more Slay the Spire 2 is more Slay the Spire 2, and I’m hopping in as soon as I can.

Monster Train 2 was one of my favorite games of last year, so I’m always glad to have a reason to jump back in. This week’s DLC, The Punished, is a perfect opportunity to do so, adding a new clan to the base game’s already packed roster. Since any clan can be combined with a second one to start a run, adding just one more option at the game’s start has an exponential effect, expanding the ways you can approach each attempt. As the DLC’s name implies, the new Punished clan gains buffs when taking damage, and you get new suite of cards that damages the whole playing field at once, harming foes and bolstering your allies. Even if you’re not checking out the DLC, the base game is absolutely worth picking up – just read my glowing review.

If you’ve been hankering for a new direction to go with your tabletop RPG group, may I recommend the incredibly versatile Cypher System from Monte Cook Games? The new Character Rulebook includes everything you need to get started, and set your adventures in virtually any fictional backdrop you can imagine, from hard sci-fi to gritty horror to high fantasy. Cypher’s polished approach to narrative-first and player-focused game sessions is much easier to pick up than many new rules systems, but it has enormous flexibility to deliver smart, creative, and exciting adventures that can help to change things up if your playing group has been in a rut.

#4082. Diablo 4’s Warlock looks like an unhinged Necromancer with Sorcerer energy in first look at gameplay

Diablo 4's practitioner of forbidden arts, The Warlock, has been officially unveiled as the second class coming with Lord of Hatred.

Thanks to a meaty, well-produced Diablo 4 Developer Update, we got to have our promised first look at gameplay of the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The showcase offered a deep look at the Warlock’s core archetypes, its gameplay and skills loop, and where the class sits within the game’s existing roster of diverse classes.

Since the initial reveal of Lord of Hatred, The Warlock has remained the mysterious second class. Anyone who pre-purchased the expansion was able to get immediate access to The Paladin, the other class arriving with the expansion. It wasn’t until February that Blizzard officially revealed the class to the world, but we had to wait until this most recent Developer Update to actually see it in action.

The Warlock’s pragmatism exists as the counterpart to The Paladin's purity, in that Warlocks don’t shy away from harnessing the powers of Hell to eliminate their enemies. The class can conjure up demons to do their bidding, and utilise attacks previously only available to legions of Hell.

The Warlock is a hybrid pet and caster class. Their gameplay revolves around summoning demons, and undermining enemies with shadow arts. They rely on two resources: Wrath, and Dominance. Casting Skills consumes Wrath, whereas Dominance is what allows the Warlock to summon and exploit demons.

The Warlock has four archetypes players can spec into. Legions are traditional summoners who rely on overwhelming numbers to crush enemies. Vanguards are closer to Sorcerers, capable of dealing damage head-on. Masterminds utilise shadowcraft to slowly drain their enemies. Finally, Ritualists are summoners of the most terrifying Hell demons.

The Warlock is able to do this by fusing Soul Shards into their bodies. Going down any of the four paths becomes available after reaching level 30, which is when the class mechanic is unlocked. Each Soul Shard is tied to a certain demon, and its through that power that the Warlock is able to call upon them in combat. Your choice does, of course, affect your abilities going forward.

Warlocks arrive alongside new Uniques that cater to their specific playstyles, which is similar to what we’ve previously seen with The Paladin, and The Spiritborn before that.

Lord of Hatred arrives April 28. While we wait, Diablo 4’s next season is kicking off next week to deliver a bit of mindless fun to hold us over until the big day.
